RC.q: According to paragraph 2 of the passage about the glucose meter, how did the father explain not using the meter?
o: He felt fine, so he saw no need for more information.
The nurse had not shown him how the meter worked.
Yard work kept him too busy to check his readings.
He did not trust the readings the meter gave him.
RC.w: Paragraph 2 says that when asked, he said he felt fine, and that feeling fine was, in his view, all the information he needed.

n.1: Contradicts paragraph 2, which says the nurse had shown him how to use the meter.
n.2: Distortion: he mowed the lawn on the day of his diagnosis (paragraph 1), but he did not give yard work as a reason.
n.3: He does not question the meter's accuracy; he simply sees no need to use it.

RC.q: As used in paragraph 3 of the passage about the glucose meter, the word 'approach' most nearly means...
o: a path leading to a building
a way of handling a problem
RC.w: The narrator 'tried an approach' the father would respect and then describes a method: the chart, no lecturing, recording the narrator's own readings where he could see them. Here 'approach' means a way of dealing with a situation.

n.0: The physical sense (the approach of a train); the narrator is not moving toward a place.
n.1: The sense used for roads ('the approach to the bridge'); nothing here is a path.
n.2: Fits the sense of approaching someone with a request, but the narrator makes no request; the paragraph stresses that the narrator 'didn't lecture.'

RC.q: Which word best describes the narrator's attitude toward the father in the passage about the glucose meter?
RC.w: The narrator respects the father's pride, notes his 'square, careful handwriting,' enjoys his engine comparisons and shares his pride at the three-month visit. The attitude is warm and affectionate.

n.0: The narrator worries but waits four days without comment; the details show patience, not impatience.
n.1: The narrator expresses no bitterness about the father's stubbornness; the closing paragraph shows understanding.
n.3: The narrator mentions the father's stubbornness without judging it; the warm details and the closing reflection show respect, not disapproval.

RC.q: What is the main idea of the passage about the glucose meter?
o: Older adults find glucose meters hard to learn to use at home.
The father managed his diabetes once he could do it his own way.
The narrator chose a nursing career because of the father's illness.
Charts are the most effective way to teach patients about diabetes.
RC.w: The story moves from the father's refusal, through the chart that let him begin on his own terms, to his ownership of his numbers, and the last paragraph says he needed a way to take charge that felt like his own idea.

n.0: Unsupported generalization: the nurse had shown him how to use the meter; his problem was willingness, not difficulty.
n.2: Unsupported: the narrator was already taking nursing prerequisites; the passage does not say the illness caused that choice.
n.3: Overgeneralization: the narrator says, 'I have since learned many better ways to teach patients.'

RC.q: Why does the narrator of the glucose meter passage most likely record a blood pressure reading on the chart each morning?
o: To model the habit without telling the father what to do
Because an anatomy course required daily blood pressure records
To show the father that the narrator's numbers were worse than his
Because the nurse had asked the family to track readings together
RC.w: Paragraph 3 says the narrator 'didn't lecture' and recorded the readings 'where he could see them,' as part of an approach the father would respect. The clues point to setting an example rather than giving orders.

n.1: Possible but unsupported: the cuff came from an anatomy kit, but the passage does not say the course required daily records.
n.2: Unsupported: the narrator's numbers are not compared with the father's anywhere in the passage.
n.3: Unsupported: the nurse is described teaching the father to use the meter, not asking the family to track readings.

RC.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the passage about the glucose meter?
o: The chart cured the father's diabetes within three months.
The nurse's warnings were what finally changed the father's mind.
The chart, not his diet, caused the father's improved results.
The father came to treat his readings as something he could manage.
RC.w: Paragraph 5 shows him starting his own chart, adding a food column and talking about what makes his numbers 'run rough' or 'run smooth,' like engines he could fix. He came to see his readings as something he could understand and manage.

n.0: Overstatement: the nurse said his results had improved; the passage does not say his diabetes was cured.
n.1: Unsupported: no warnings from the nurse are described; the change follows the chart on the refrigerator.
n.2: Causal overreach: he also began tracking what he ate, and the passage cannot separate the effects of the chart and his diet.

RC.q: Which title best fits the passage about fever?
o: How the Immune System Protects the Body
The Hypothalamus: The Brain's Built-In Thermostat
When a Fever Becomes a Medical Emergency
Fever: How and Why the Body Turns Up the Heat
RC.w: The passage explains how a fever starts and ends (paragraphs 2 and 4) and why the body raises its temperature (paragraph 3), presenting fever as a sign of defense. This title names the topic and reflects that main idea.

n.0: Too broad: the passage covers one defense, fever, not the immune system's full set of protections.
n.1: Too narrow: the hypothalamus is the focus of paragraph 2 alone.
n.2: Too narrow and off-center: only paragraph 5 mentions when a fever needs prompt care, and the passage mostly presents fever as useful.

RC.q: According to paragraph 2 of the fever passage, why does a person with a rising fever often feel chilled?
o: Sweat on the skin cools the body as the fever begins.
The brain's raised set point makes the body seem too cold.
Widened blood vessels in the skin let heat escape the body.
White blood cells draw heat away from the skin to fight germs.
RC.w: Paragraph 2 says chemical messengers raise the hypothalamus's set point, so the brain treats the body as too cold for the new target. That is why the person feels chilled while the skin feels warm to others.

n.0: Wrong stage: sweating happens when the fever breaks (paragraph 4), not as it begins.
n.2: Reversal: during a rising fever, skin vessels narrow to hold in heat; they widen when the fever breaks.
n.3: The passage says some white blood cells work faster in warmth; it does not say they draw heat from the skin.

RC.q: How does paragraph 4 of the fever passage relate to paragraph 2?
o: It describes the reverse of the process in paragraph 2.
It offers a solution to the problem in paragraph 2.
It gives an example that supports paragraph 2's claim.
It presents a view that disputes paragraph 2's account.
RC.w: Paragraph 2 explains how a fever rises (set point up, skin vessels narrow, shivering); paragraph 4 explains how it falls (set point down, vessels widen, sweating). Paragraph 4 runs the same process in reverse.

n.1: Problem-and-solution trap: paragraph 2 describes a normal defense, not a problem, and paragraph 4 describes what the body does next, not a fix.
n.2: Paragraph 4 describes a new stage of the process, not an example of something stated in paragraph 2.
n.3: Paragraph 4 agrees with paragraph 2; the two fit together as stages of one process.

RC.q: As used in paragraph 4 of the fever passage, saying a fever has 'broken' means that the fever...
o: has begun to go back down
RC.w: Paragraph 4 links 'broken' to the moment sweating begins, after the set point returns to normal and the body starts shedding heat. The fever is starting to go down.

n.0: Near miss: the peak comes just before the set point drops, but 'broken' marks the start of cooling, when sweating begins.
n.1: This reads 'broken' as damage; the paragraph describes a normal step in recovery.
n.3: Medicine is not mentioned in paragraph 4; the phrase refers to the body shedding heat.

RC.q: Which statement can be inferred from paragraph 5 of the fever passage?
o: Fever-reducing medicines do more harm than good in healthy adults.
Infants usually develop higher fevers than older adults do.
A moderate fever calls for prompt care in most healthy adults.
The same fever may call for different responses in different people.
RC.w: Paragraph 5 says infants, older adults and people with weakened immune systems may need prompt care even for a moderate fever, while a mild fever in a healthy adult is usually a clue that the body is fighting back. Together these imply that the right response depends partly on who has the fever.

n.0: Contradicts the paragraph, which says many doctors recommend these medicines for comfort.
n.1: The paragraph says infants may need prompt care, not that their fevers run higher; that idea needs outside knowledge.
n.2: Overgeneralization: prompt care for a moderate fever is linked to infants, older adults and people with weakened immunity, not to most healthy adults.

RC.q: What is the author's primary purpose in the passage about fever?
o: To explain how and why the body raises its temperature in infection
To persuade readers to stop taking medicine that lowers a fever
To describe one patient's experience of a high fever and recovery
To warn readers that high fevers often cause lasting harm to health
RC.w: The passage explains the mechanism (set point, shivering, sweating) and the reasons (slowing germs, speeding white blood cells) in neutral language. Its purpose is to inform.

n.1: The passage says many doctors recommend these medicines for comfort; it does not argue against them.
n.2: No individual patient appears; the passage describes fever in general terms.
n.3: Paragraph 5 notes that very high temperatures can be dangerous, but one caution is not the purpose of the whole passage, and 'often cause lasting harm' overstates it.

RC.q: According to the passage about food safety, why should a large pot of soup be divided before it is refrigerated?
o: A large pot can raise the refrigerator's temperature.
Bacteria double every 20 minutes inside a refrigerator.
Its center can stay warm for hours in a deep pot.
Shallow containers keep soup safe for several weeks.
RC.w: Paragraph 3: a large pot 'may stay warm in its center for hours, because heat escapes slowly from a deep container'.

n.0: True but unstated: plausible in real life, but the passage gives a different reason.
n.1: Distortion: the 20-minute doubling applies in the danger zone, 40°F to 140°F, not in a cold refrigerator.
n.3: Unsupported: the passage gives no storage time for leftovers.

RC.q: Which is the best summary of the passage about food safety at home?
o: The USDA lists three safe ways to thaw frozen food: in the refrigerator, in cold water that is changed every 30 minutes, or in the microwave oven.
About 48 million Americans get foodborne illness each year, which shows that home cooks are careless and need strict new government food rules.
Because many bacteria double in 20 minutes, any food left in the danger zone for even a short time should be thrown out rather than chilled.
Bacteria multiply quickly between 40°F and 140°F, so cooks should chill food promptly in shallow containers, thaw it safely and cook it to safe temperatures.
RC.w: The key covers the danger zone (1-2), quick cooling (3), safe thawing (4) and thermometer temperatures (5), with no new claims.

n.0: Covers only paragraph 4.
n.1: Adds a judgment and a recommendation the author does not make.
n.2: Contradicts the passage, which allows up to two hours (one hour above 90°F) before refrigerating.

RC.q: As used in paragraph 4 of the food safety passage, the word "weak" most nearly means
RC.w: 'Thawing is another weak point': a stage where food is open to danger because the surface can warm into the danger zone.

n.1: Physical sense: lacking bodily strength, which does not fit a step in food handling.
n.2: Other sense: weak coffee or tea, which does not fit thawing.
n.3: Other sense: a weak argument; the paragraph is not judging an argument.

RC.q: Based on paragraph 4 of the food safety passage, which inference about a roast thawed on the counter is best supported?
o: It is safe on the counter if it weighs under 4 pounds.
Its center warms into the danger zone before its surface.
It can be safely refrozen once it has thawed completely.
It may be unsafe even while part of it is still frozen.
RC.w: The outside 'can warm into the danger zone while its center is still icy', so a partly frozen roast can still have a surface where bacteria multiply.

n.0: Overreach: the 4 to 5 pound figure is the refrigerator thawing rate, not a safe size for counter thawing.
n.1: Reversal: the outside warms first while the center stays icy.
n.2: Outside knowledge: the passage says nothing about refreezing.

RC.q: Which conclusion about home food safety is best supported by the passage?
o: Most foodborne illness in the United States begins in home kitchens.
Controlling time and temperature at home lowers the risk of foodborne illness.
Food that still smells normal is safe to eat after sitting out overnight.
Microwave thawing is the safest of the three methods the USDA lists.
RC.w: Every paragraph turns on time and temperature: the danger zone and the two-hour rule, quick cooling, safe thawing and cooking temperatures.

n.0: Overgeneralization: the passage says only that not every case begins in a restaurant.
n.2: Contradiction: food in the danger zone 'may look and smell normal' and still make someone sick.
n.3: Unsupported: the three methods are all called safe, and none is ranked safest.

RC.q: Which statement from the passage on food safety expresses an opinion?
o: Within it, many bacteria can double in number in as little as 20 minutes.
Planning a meal a day ahead is a small price to pay for that peace of mind.
Poultry is safe to eat once it reaches an internal temperature of 165°F.
The refrigerator method is the slowest, needing about a day for every 4 to 5 pounds of food.
RC.w: 'A small price to pay' is a value judgment: whether the planning is worth it cannot be proven, and readers could disagree.

n.0: Fact: a measurable claim that can be checked by laboratory evidence.
n.2: Fact: a published safety standard that can be verified.
n.3: Fact: thawing times can be measured and compared.

RC.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage about the Apgar score?
o: Before the 1950s, staff focused on the mother, so a newborn in distress could go unnoticed for several minutes.
Virginia Apgar designed a newborn score that could predict a child's long-term health from the first minute of life.
Apgar's quick five-sign score gave birth attendants a shared way to judge newborns and find those needing help.
By turning a newborn's condition into a number, the score let researchers compare practices used during labor.
RC.w: The passage moves from the problem (no shared method, paragraph 1) to Apgar's five-sign score (paragraph 2), its speed and common language (paragraph 3), its narrow purpose of flagging babies who need help (paragraph 4) and its use today (paragraph 5). Only this statement covers that whole arc.

n.0: Too narrow: this is the background in paragraph 1, not the point the whole passage makes.
n.1: Opposite: paragraph 4 says the score was not designed to predict long-term health or intelligence.
n.3: Too narrow: the research benefit is one effect described in paragraph 4.

RC.q: According to the passage, why did repeating the Apgar score at five minutes become standard?
o: A second score showed whether the newborn's condition was improving.
Apgar found that one-minute scores were too hurried to be accurate.
Researchers needed two scores to link labor practices to outcomes.
The five-minute score predicted a child's later health more closely.
RC.w: Paragraph 3 says the five-minute score became standard "because the second score showed whether a baby was improving."

n.1: The passage never questions the one-minute score; it praises the score's speed as its main appeal.
n.2: Paragraph 4 links research to recording the score as a number, not to taking a second score.
n.3: Paragraph 4 says the score was not designed to predict long-term health; this reason is not in the passage.

RC.q: According to the passage, which event came after Apgar proposed her scoring system but before the five-minute score became standard?
o: Apgar noticed newborns being described in vague terms.
Apgar watched many births from beside the operating table.
The score came into use in hospitals around the world.
Apgar's scoring method appeared in published form.
RC.w: Paragraph 2 says Apgar proposed the score in 1952 and published it "the following year"; paragraph 3 says the five-minute score became standard "later." Publication falls between the two events.

n.0: Her observation of vague descriptions came before the proposal; it is what led her to create the score.
n.1: Watching births from the operating table came before the proposal and prompted it.
n.2: Worldwide use is described in paragraph 5 as the situation today, after the five-minute score was standard.

RC.q: As used in paragraph 3 of the passage about the Apgar score, the word "appeal" most nearly means
RC.w: Paragraph 3 explains what made the system attractive: it was fast, needed no special equipment and gave staff a common language. "Appeal" here is the quality that draws people to something.

n.0: A formal challenge is the legal sense (an appeal of a court ruling), which does not fit a scoring system.
n.2: An urgent request ("an appeal for help") is a common sense of the word, but the paragraph is describing the system's advantages, not asking for anything.
n.3: "Public demand" fits the sentence loosely but changes its meaning: the paragraph explains why the system worked well, not how much people asked for it.

RC.q: What can be inferred from paragraphs 1 and 2 about how newborns were assessed before Apgar's score?
o: Most newborns who struggled to breathe at birth did not survive their first hour of life.
Doctors refused to examine newborns until the mother was out of danger after the birth.
Two staff members could judge one newborn differently, with no shared measure.
Staff relied on special equipment that most hospitals could not afford.
RC.w: Paragraph 1 says there was "no shared, quick method" for judging newborns, and paragraph 2 says staff used vague terms such as "fine" or "a little weak." Without a shared standard, two people could describe the same baby differently and have no common measure to settle it.

n.0: Overstatement: the passage says struggling babies could go unnoticed, but it gives no survival figures.
n.1: "Refused" goes beyond the passage, which says only that staff focused on the mother.
n.3: Paragraph 3 says Apgar's score needed no special equipment; nothing suggests that earlier methods depended on costly devices.

RC.q: What is the most likely reason the author included paragraph 4 in the passage about the Apgar score?
o: To clarify the limits of the score's purpose and note a wider benefit
To argue that the score should be used to predict later development
To describe the five signs checked by the person attending the birth
To show that later doctors found serious flaws in Apgar's method
RC.w: Paragraph 4 first states what the score was not designed to do and what its narrower purpose was, then explains its added value for research. Its job in the passage is to set limits and add a broader effect.

n.1: Paragraph 4 says the opposite: medical groups caution against using the score to predict long-term health.
n.2: Wrong paragraph: the five signs are listed in paragraph 2.
n.3: The caution in paragraph 4 is about misusing the score for prediction, not about a flaw found in Apgar's method.

RC.q: What is the main idea of the passage about lead in older homes?
o: Old lead paint can quietly harm young children, but families can take steps to reduce the risk.
The United States banned lead-based paint for homes in 1978 after many years of widespread use.
Children under 6 swallow more household dust than adults do because of the ways they play.
Renovating an older home is too dangerous for families to attempt while children live there.
RC.w: The passage explains where old lead paint remains (1), why young children are most at risk (2), how lead harms them without obvious signs (3), and how cleaning, repairs, certified renovators and testing lower the risk (4-5). This statement covers all of it.

n.1: Too narrow: background from paragraph 1.
n.2: Too narrow: one supporting detail from paragraph 2.
n.3: Overstatement of paragraph 5, which says renovation needs care and certified contractors, not that it cannot be done.

RC.q: According to the passage about lead in older homes, why is a blood test needed to know whether a child has been exposed to lead?
o: Lead dust from worn paint settles on floors and windowsills.
Health agencies have not identified a safe blood lead level for children.
Much of the damage that lead causes to the brain cannot be undone.
Most children with raised lead levels look and act healthy.
RC.w: Paragraph 3: "most children with raised lead levels look and act healthy, so a blood test is the one reliable way to know." Because there are usually no visible signs, testing is needed.

n.0: A detail from paragraph 2 about how exposure happens, not why a test is needed to detect it.
n.1: A true detail from paragraph 3, but it explains why any level matters, not why a test is the way to find out.
n.2: A true detail from paragraph 3 about the harm, not the reason the passage gives for testing.

RC.q: Which is the best summary of the passage about lead in older homes?
o: Lead made paint durable and quick to dry. It was banned for homes in 1978, but many older homes still have it under newer layers, and window frames and doors are the surfaces most likely to release dust as they rub together.

Lead paint in older homes is dangerous to everyone, so it should be scraped off as soon as it is found. Children in these homes need regular blood tests, and families should put off any renovation until their children are grown.

Lead paint remains in many pre-1978 homes and is hazardous when worn or disturbed. Young children take in the most dust, and lead can harm their brains without visible signs. Cleaning, repairs, certified renovators and testing reduce the risk.

Lead harms the developing brain, lowering test scores and shortening attention spans. Because much of this damage cannot be undone and no safe level is known, a blood test is the most important step any parent can take.
RC.w: A summary restates the main point of every paragraph in order and adds nothing: where lead paint remains and when it is dangerous (1), why children are at risk (2), hidden harm (3), and ways to reduce risk (4-5). This option does that.

n.0: Covers only paragraphs 1 and 2 and dwells on minor details; the harm and the ways to reduce risk are missing.
n.1: Contradicts the passage: paragraph 1 says intact paint poses little danger, paragraph 4 says peeling paint should not be scraped, and paragraph 5 describes how to renovate safely.
n.3: Centers on paragraph 3 and adds a judgment the author does not make; prevention steps are left out.

RC.q: As used in paragraph 1 of the passage about lead in older homes, the word 'disturbed' most nearly means
RC.w: Paint that "chips, peels or is disturbed" releases lead; paragraph 5 gives examples such as sanding and scraping. Here disturbed means physically moved or broken up.

n.0: A common meaning for people, but paint cannot be emotionally upset.
n.2: The "do not disturb" sense applies to a person resting, not to paint.
n.3: Paint left exposed is not the same as paint that has been worked on or broken apart.

RC.q: Which word best describes the author's tone in the passage about lead in older homes?
RC.w: The author alerts readers to a hidden risk ("no safe blood lead level," "cannot be undone," "look and act healthy") and gives steps to take. Warning the reader about a risk while offering precautions is a cautionary tone.

n.1: Tone matched to the topic: lead damage is serious, but the author offers practical ways to lower the risk.
n.2: Too strong: the author does not express anger at anyone; the warnings are calm.
n.3: The author shows no mixed feelings; the message is consistent throughout.

RC.q: What can be inferred from paragraph 2 of the passage about lead in older homes about painted windows that are opened and closed often?
o: Their movement lets fresh air carry lead dust safely outdoors.
Their frames contain more lead than any other painted surface.
They should be replaced before a young child moves into the home.
Their frames may shed more lead dust than walls that are left alone.
RC.w: Paragraph 2 says paint releases dust when it wears down, "especially on surfaces that rub together, such as window frames." Windows that are used often rub more, so they are likely to release more dust than untouched walls.

n.0: Not supported: the passage says the dust settles on floors and windowsills.
n.1: Overstatement: the passage says these surfaces wear and release dust, not that they hold more lead.
n.2: Advice the passage never gives; paragraph 4 recommends cleaning and repair.

RC.q: As used in paragraph 3 of the passage about quiet hours on a hospital unit, the word "stable" most nearly means
RC.w: The sentence contrasts "stable patients" with patients whose "condition required" waking. "Stable" describes a medical condition that is steady and not worsening.

n.1: Calm describes mood; the sentence is about the patient's medical condition, which decides whether waking is needed.
n.2: "Fixed in one place" is the sense used for objects (a stable ladder), not for a patient's condition.
n.3: "Strong and healthy" loosely fits, but a stable patient may still be quite ill; the word means the illness is steady.

RC.q: Which title best fits the passage about nighttime noise on a hospital unit?
o: Why Patients Sleep Poorly in Hospitals
Quieting the Night on One Hospital Unit
How One Unit Cut Sleep Medication Requests
Proof That Quiet Hours Speed Patient Recovery
RC.w: The passage describes one unit's noise problem, its quiet-hours program, the results and the team's caution about them. A title naming the unit's effort to quiet its nights covers all five paragraphs.

n.0: Too narrow: the general problem of hospital sleep is only the introduction in paragraph 1.
n.2: Too narrow: the drop in sleep medication requests is one result reported in paragraph 4.
n.3: Overstatement: paragraph 5 says the survey was not a controlled experiment, and recovery was never measured.

RC.q: According to the passage, what share of patients rated their sleep as poor or very poor after quiet hours began?
RC.w: Paragraph 4: "The share of patients rating their sleep as poor or very poor fell to 37 percent."

n.0: 61 percent is the share before quiet hours began (paragraph 2).
n.1: 24 is the size of the drop in percentage points (61 minus 37), not the share after the change.
n.2: 49 is the average nighttime noise level in decibels after the change, not a share of patients.

RC.q: Based on paragraph 5, the team most likely plans to repeat its measurements on two other units because it
o: has concluded that the family lounge caused most of the change
found that its first measurements were recorded incorrectly
wants to learn whether similar results appear beyond one unit
expects the other units to be quieter than the first unit was
RC.w: Paragraph 5 lists reasons the first results are uncertain (no controlled design, different patients, the new lounge) and then says the team will measure two more units. Gathering results from more units is the step that addresses those doubts.

n.0: Overreach: the lounge is named as one possible influence, not as the cause of most of the change.
n.1: Nothing in the passage questions the accuracy of the sound meters or the survey records.
n.3: The passage gives no information about noise levels on the other units.

RC.q: Which conclusion about the quiet-hours program is best supported by the information in the passage?
o: It helped patients on the unit recover from their illnesses more quickly than before.
It lowered nighttime noise to a level at which most patients on the unit slept well.
It showed, through fewer medication requests, that patients needed less pain relief.
Noise and poor sleep ratings fell after it began, though other factors may have helped.
RC.w: Paragraph 4 reports lower noise, fewer poor sleep ratings and fewer medication requests. Paragraph 5 notes that the survey was not controlled, the patients differed and a family lounge opened in the same months. The supported conclusion reports the improvement while allowing that other factors may have contributed.

n.0: Recovery was never measured; paragraph 1 says only that poor sleep may slow recovery.
n.1: Misreads the numbers: 37 percent still rated their sleep poor or very poor, and a rating that is not poor is not the same as sleeping well.
n.2: The passage reports requests for sleep medication, not pain relief; linking the two goes beyond the evidence.

RC.q: Which statement based on the passage about quiet hours expresses an opinion rather than a fact?
o: On the morning survey, 61 percent of patients rated their sleep as poor or very poor.
Quiet hours were the most worthwhile change the staff had made in years.
The survey was not designed by the team as a controlled experiment.
Peaks above 80 decibels occurred several times each night.
RC.w: "Most worthwhile" is a judgment that others could reasonably dispute and that no measurement can prove. It is the nurse manager's opinion, reported in paragraph 5.

n.0: The statement contains the words "poor" and "very poor," but it reports what the survey found, which can be checked against the survey records.
n.2: Whether a survey was designed as a controlled experiment can be verified from how it was set up.
n.3: Noise peaks were recorded by sound meters, so this statement can be checked.

RC.q: According to the passage about Daniel Hale Williams, why did he found Provident Hospital?
o: He needed a hospital where he could perform surgery on the chest.
Black patients and Black nursing students were being shut out elsewhere.
The Chicago hospital where he had trained closed during the 1880s.
Freedmen's Hospital asked him to open a branch in Chicago.
RC.w: Paragraph 3: Black patients were often refused care or treated poorly, and Black women were shut out of nursing schools; in 1891 Williams "answered both problems at once" by founding Provident.

n.0: Reverses the order: the chest operation came two years after he founded Provident.
n.2: Not stated: the passage says nothing about any hospital closing.
n.3: Wrong order: Williams joined Freedmen's in 1894, three years after founding Provident.

RC.q: Which statement best describes how the passage about Daniel Hale Williams is organized?
o: It compares Williams's surgery with the methods of other surgeons of his time.
It presents his life in strict time order, from his birth to his death.
It opens with an event from 1893, then returns to his youth and moves forward.
It describes several problems in hospitals, each followed by his solution.
RC.w: Paragraph 1 describes the 1893 operation; paragraph 2 jumps back to his birth in 1856; paragraphs 3-5 move forward through 1891, 1894, 1895, 1913 and 1931. Order of mention differs from order of occurrence at the start.

n.0: Other surgeons are mentioned once in paragraph 1; no point-by-point comparison is made.
n.1: The passage begins in 1893, not with his birth, so it is not in strict time order.
n.3: Paragraph 3 presents problems and his response, but the passage as a whole follows his life over time.

RC.q: As used in paragraph 3 of the passage about Daniel Hale Williams, the word 'answered' most nearly means
RC.w: Williams "answered both problems at once by founding Provident Hospital": he dealt with, or addressed, the problems through action.

n.1: The everyday sense of answering a letter; nothing was written in reply.
n.2: Williams opposed the conditions he saw; he did not agree with them.
n.3: Confuses "answered" with "answered for," meaning to be held responsible.

RC.q: Which word best describes the author's attitude toward Daniel Hale Williams?
RC.w: Word choice shows high regard: he chose "with remarkable courage" to operate, and his institutions, built "with such tireless energy," may be his "most lasting gift." That is an admiring attitude.

n.0: The author never questions Williams's achievements.
n.1: The author notes early hardship, but the passage dwells on his accomplishments rather than on pity for his difficulties.
n.3: The author does not long for the past; the passage describes 1893 surgery as deadly and limited.

RC.q: Why does the author most likely mention in paragraph 1 that X-rays, safe transfusions and antibiotics were not yet available?
o: To explain why Cornish needed several weeks to recover in the hospital
To show how great a risk Williams took by operating inside the chest
To suggest that Williams later helped develop these medical tools
To compare surgery in Chicago with surgery in other cities of the time
RC.w: The detail sits between "such operations [were] deadly" and "chose with remarkable courage to operate anyway": it shows how few tools surgeons had, and so how risky the operation was.

n.0: The passage does not connect these missing tools to the length of Cornish's recovery.
n.2: Not supported: the passage never says Williams worked on any of these tools.
n.3: No other city is mentioned; the detail describes surgery in general at the time.

RC.q: Which title best fits the passage about Daniel Hale Williams?
o: Daniel Hale Williams and the History of Heart Surgery
Daniel Hale Williams's Years at Freedmen's Hospital
Pioneers Who Opened Medicine to Everyone
Daniel Hale Williams: Surgeon and Builder of Institutions
RC.w: The passage presents a daring 1893 operation (1), Williams's path into medicine (2), and the hospitals, training programs and professional groups he founded or led (3-5), ending with the claim that these may be his most lasting gift. The title names both sides of that main idea.

n.0: Off center: the passage describes one operation, not the history of heart surgery.
n.1: Too narrow: Freedmen's Hospital is one detail in paragraph 4.
n.2: Too broad: the passage is about one physician, and this title would fit a whole book.

RC.q: According to the passage, how can hearing aids make tinnitus less bothersome?
o: They give the brain more outside sound to process.
They repair hair cells that loud noise has damaged.
They play soft background noise at bedtime.
They train the listener to shift attention away.
RC.w: Paragraph 4 states that hearing aids help "because amplifying outside sounds gives the brain more to process."

n.1: Contradicts paragraph 2: damaged hair cells "do not grow back," and the passage gives hearing aids no repair role.
n.2: Wrong detail: this describes sound generators, a different approach in paragraph 4.
n.3: Wrong detail: shifting attention is what counseling approaches teach, not hearing aids.

RC.q: Which title best fits the passage about tinnitus?
o: How Loud Noise Damages Inner Ear Cells
New Treatments That Cure Ringing Ears
RC.w: The passage defines tinnitus and explains its causes (paragraphs 1-3), ways to make it less bothersome (paragraph 4) and how to prevent it (paragraph 5). This title names the topic and covers every part.

n.0: Too narrow: hair-cell damage is the subject of paragraph 2 only and leaves out other causes, management and prevention.
n.1: Contradicts paragraph 4, which says no single treatment silences tinnitus for everyone; the approaches make it less bothersome.
n.3: Off center: age-related hearing loss is one cause listed in paragraph 3, not the subject of the passage.

RC.q: As used in paragraph 2 of the passage about tinnitus, the word "trigger" most nearly means
RC.w: Paragraph 2 calls inner-ear damage 'the most common trigger' of tinnitus and then explains how that damage leads to ringing; paragraph 3 continues 'Noise is not the only cause.' A trigger here is a cause that sets the symptom off.

n.0: The literal sense of the word; nothing in the paragraph is a firearm part.
n.1: Loose fit: paragraph 5 calls brief ringing a warning, but here the damage produces the tinnitus; it does not warn of it.
n.2: Reversal: tinnitus is the effect; the damage is what brings it on.

RC.q: Which word best describes the author's tone in the passage about tinnitus?
RC.w: The author explains causes, treatments and prevention clearly and evenly, with practical advice but no strong emotion: an informative tone.

n.1: Too strong: the author calls brief ringing "a warning" but writes calmly and offers ways to cope.
n.2: Tone matched to the topic: although no single cure exists, the author stresses that many people find relief and that prevention works.
n.3: The author does not doubt any claim or treatment; the approaches in paragraph 4 are presented as helpful.

RC.q: Which inference about noise-related tinnitus is best supported by paragraphs 1 and 2?
o: It results from reduced activity in the brain's hearing centers.
It can last because the damaged hair cells are not replaced.
It usually fades once the hair cells have had time to regrow.
It starts when the cochlea sends stronger signals to the brain.
RC.w: Paragraph 2 says noise breaks hair cells and "they do not grow back," and paragraph 1 says for some people the ringing lingers or never leaves. Together they support the inference that the condition can be lasting because the damage is permanent.

n.0: Reversal: paragraph 2 says the hearing centers "may become more active," not less.
n.2: Contradicts paragraph 2: the hair cells do not grow back.
n.3: Reversal: paragraph 2 says fewer signals arrive from the ear.

RC.q: Which statement from the passage about tinnitus is an opinion?
o: Loud noise can bend or break these cells, and they do not grow back.
Tinnitus may be heard in one ear or both.
Certain medications and head injuries can produce tinnitus.
Prevention is by far the wisest approach.
RC.w: "By far the wisest" is a value judgment that cannot be proven and that others could dispute; it is an opinion.

n.0: A fact: physical damage to hair cells can be verified by research.
n.1: A fact: where the sound is heard can be checked by asking and testing patients.
n.2: A fact: a verifiable claim about causes, with no judgment word.

RC.q: As used in paragraph 4 of the passage about school nurses, the word 'spread' most nearly means
RC.w: The phased plan adds three nurses next year "and the rest over the following two years," so to spread the cost is to divide it over a longer period.

n.0: The plan adds nurses in steps, but spreading the cost does not make it grow; it divides the same cost across years.
n.2: A cost can be spread among people, but the sentence divides it across years, and taxpayers are never mentioned.
n.3: The sense used for butter or paint; it does not fit a budget plan.

RC.q: Which word best describes the author's tone in the passage about school nurses?
RC.w: The author presses for action before a deadline ("I urge every parent... to attend that meeting or write to the board before then") and stresses that a nurse may be twenty minutes away when a child needs one. That is an urgent tone.

n.0: Too strong: the author is not angry; the author thanks the secretary and concedes that the cost is real.
n.1: The statistics serve an argument; a passage built around "should," "deserve" and "I urge" is not neutral.
n.2: The author proposes a phased plan and expects it to work, not a bad outcome.

RC.q: Which inference about the eight schools without a full-time nurse is best supported by paragraph 2?
o: Their students have fewer long-term health conditions than students elsewhere.
Their traveling nurses are less qualified than the nurses at the other schools.
Their principals have asked the board to hire nurses for their buildings.
A child there may need care at a time when no nurse is in the building.
RC.w: Paragraph 2 says the eight schools share two traveling nurses, so a nurse may be twenty minutes or more away when a child needs one. It follows that a child may need care while no nurse is present.

n.0: A possible reason for how nurses are assigned, but the passage gives district-wide totals, not figures for these schools.
n.1: Not supported: the passage says nothing about the nurses' training.
n.2: Not supported: the passage names no requests from principals.

RC.q: Based on paragraph 4 of the passage about school nurses, which conclusion would the author most likely agree with?
o: Hiring nurses costs money, but going without them also costs money and class time.
The district should hire all eight nurses next year, even if other programs must be cut.
Substitute teachers cost the district more each year than a full-time nurse does.
Board members who object to the cost care less about students than about budgets.
RC.w: The author concedes that "the cost is real" but argues that the district already pays for substitutes and pays "in lost learning" when students are sent home. The conclusion that both choices have costs combines those points.

n.1: Contradicts the phased plan in paragraph 4: three nurses next year and the rest over two more years.
n.2: Not supported: the passage gives the cost of a nurse but no yearly figure for substitutes, so no comparison is possible.
n.3: Not supported: the author answers the board members' argument and concedes their point about cost without questioning their motives.

RC.q: What is the author's primary purpose in the passage about school nurses?
o: To inform readers how many district students have asthma, diabetes or severe allergies
To praise the school secretary who helped a wheezing second grader recover
To persuade readers to support placing a nurse in every school in the district
To explain the range of duties a school nurse carries out during a school day
RC.w: The author makes a claim (every school needs a nurse), supports it with an anecdote, numbers and a cost argument, answers an objection, and ends with a call to action: "I urge every parent...to attend that meeting or write to the board." That is persuasion.

n.0: The statistics in paragraph 2 are evidence for the argument; informing readers of them is not the purpose of the whole passage.
n.1: The secretary is thanked in paragraph 1, but the story is used to show that she should not have been the most qualified person present.
n.3: Paragraph 3 lists duties to support the argument; it is one part, not the purpose of the whole passage.

RC.q: Which statement from the passage about school nurses expresses an opinion?
o: Our children deserve a nurse down the hall, not across town.
This year, district records list 214 students with asthma.
The other eight share two nurses who travel between buildings.
Last spring, a second grader at Lincoln Elementary began wheezing during recess.
RC.w: "Deserve" expresses a value judgment about what children should have; it cannot be proven true or false, and others could reasonably disagree.

n.1: A number from district records that can be checked, so it is a fact.
n.2: A verifiable statement about how nurses are assigned.
n.3: An event that witnesses and school records could confirm.

VO.q: The surgeon removed the malignant growth along with a margin of healthy tissue. As used in this sentence, what does the word "malignant" mean?
VO.w: Malignant means likely to spread and worsen; cancerous.

n.0: Poorly nourished is malnourished, a look-alike beginning with mal-.
n.1: Inflamed tissue is red and swollen; malignant means cancerous.
n.2: Harmless is benign, the opposite.

VO.q: Because the infant could not swallow tablets, her medication was given as a buccal gel. What is the best definition of the word "buccal" in this sentence?
VO.w: Buccal means relating to the cheek: a buccal medicine is placed between the cheek and gum to absorb.

n.0: A nose route is nasal; buccal refers to the cheek.
n.1: Under the tongue is sublingual, the other mouth route.
n.2: This route also avoids swallowing, but it is rectal, not buccal.

VO.q: During the bus crash response, the charge nurse began triage as the first ambulances arrived. What is the best definition of the word "triage" in this sentence?
VO.w: Triage means sorting patients by how urgently they need care so the most critical are treated first.

n.0: Transfer fits a mass-casualty scene loosely, but triage is the sorting itself.
n.2: Registering arrivals fits the scene loosely, but it is not the meaning of triage.
n.3: Treatment follows triage; triage decides who is treated first.

VO.q: She worked three consecutive night shifts and then had four days off. What is the best definition of the word consecutive in this sentence?
VO.w: Consecutive means following one after another without a break.

n.0: Spread out is the opposite of back-to-back.
n.1: At the same time is concurrent, the look-alike.
n.3: Extra shifts are a topic fit, but consecutive describes order, not pay.

VO.q: On the pediatric unit, music therapy is used as an adjunct to pain medication. What is the best definition of the word "adjunct" in this sentence?
VO.w: An adjunct is something added to the main treatment to support it: the music therapy is used together with the medication.

n.1: Prevention is prophylaxis; an adjunct supports a main treatment.
n.2: A substitute replaces the medication; an adjunct is added alongside it.
n.3: This confuses adjunct with adjacent, meaning next to.

VO.q: After sliding into second base, Jamal had an abrasion on his knee that the trainer rinsed and covered. What is the best definition of the word "abrasion" in this sentence?
VO.w: An abrasion is a scrape that rubs away the surface of the skin, typical of sliding on dirt.

n.1: A torn, jagged cut is a laceration.
n.2: A bruise is a contusion, with no broken skin to rinse.
n.3: A pocket of pus is an abscess, a look-alike word.

VO.q: A quiet, dark room is conducive to sleep for most patients recovering after surgery. What is the best definition of the word conducive in this sentence?
VO.w: Conducive (to) means making an outcome likely; favorable.

n.0: Harmful is the opposite.
n.1: Carrying heat or electricity is conductive, the look-alike.
n.2: Necessary is too strong: a dark room helps sleep but is not required.

VO.q: After years without an accident, the roofing crew grew complacent about checking their harnesses. What is the best definition of the word complacent in this sentence?
VO.w: Complacent means self-satisfied and unaware of possible danger.

n.0: Eager to please is complaisant, another look-alike.
n.1: Willing to obey is compliant, a look-alike with nearly the opposite effect.
n.3: Fatigue could cause lapses, a topic fit, but complacent means smug, not tired.

VO.q: The instructor asked each student to explain the rationale for choosing a particular care plan. What is the best definition of the word rationale in this sentence?
VO.w: Rationale (a noun) means the reasons that explain an action or belief.

n.0: The written steps are the plan itself; the rationale is why it was chosen.
n.1: The result is the outcome, not the reasons behind the choice.
n.2: A fixed share is a ration, a look-alike.

VO.q: A mild erythema appeared around the injection site, but the area was not warm or swollen. As used in this sentence, what does the word "erythema" mean?
VO.w: Erythema is redness of the skin (erythr- = red).

n.0: An itchy, dry rash is eczema, a sound-alike.
n.1: A bruise is a contusion; erythema is redness, not bleeding under the skin.
n.2: Fluid swelling is edema, a look-alike word; the sentence also says the area was not swollen.

VO.q: Nurses and pharmacists collaborate to review each patient's medications before discharge. What is the best definition of the word collaborate in this sentence?
VO.w: Collaborate means to work together.

n.0: Competing is the opposite of working together.
n.2: Adding detail is elaborate, another look-alike.
n.3: Confirming with evidence is corroborate, the classic look-alike.

VO.q: During the pandemic, hospitals on several continents faced shortages of masks and ventilators. What is the best definition of the word "pandemic" in this sentence?
VO.w: A pandemic is an outbreak of disease that spreads across countries or the world.

n.0: Constant local presence is endemic.
n.2: Wild chaos is pandemonium, a look-alike.
n.3: An outbreak in one community is an epidemic.

VO.q: After a long flight, a patient developed pain and redness in her calf, and an ultrasound confirmed thrombophlebitis. Using all of its word parts, what does thrombophlebitis mean?
o: Vein hardening caused by a blood clot
Surgical removal of a clot in a vein
Vein inflammation with a blood clot
Artery inflammation with a blood clot
VO.w: Step 1: thromb/o means clot and phleb/o means vein. Step 2: -itis means inflammation. Together: inflammation of a vein associated with a blood clot.

n.0: Hardening is -sclerosis; -itis means inflammation.
n.1: Removal is -ectomy (thrombectomy); -itis means inflammation.
n.3: Artery is arteri/o; phleb/o means vein.

VO.q: Wearing a supportive brace can mitigate the strain on an injured knee during exercise. What is the best definition of the word "mitigate" in this sentence?
VO.w: Mitigate means to make something less severe or serious: the brace reduces the strain on the knee.

n.0: This confuses mitigate with migrate, to move from one place to another.
n.2: Increasing the strain is the opposite of mitigate.
n.3: Measuring fits the sentence loosely, but mitigate means to make less severe.

VO.q: Her blood sugar readings tended to fluctuate when she skipped breakfast and ate late at night. What is the best definition of the word fluctuate in this sentence?
VO.w: Fluctuate means to rise and fall irregularly.

n.0: A steady climb moves in one direction; fluctuate means moving up and down.
n.2: A sharp drop is one movement in one direction; fluctuate means irregular rises and falls.
n.3: Staying steady is the opposite of fluctuate (stabilize).

VO.q: The belligerent visitor shouted at the security guard and refused to leave the unit. What is the best definition of the word "belligerent" in this sentence?
VO.w: Belligerent means hostile and aggressive, eager to fight or argue, as the shouting and refusal to leave show.

n.0: Confusion could explain the refusal, but belligerent means hostile.
n.2: Shouting fits loudness, but belligerent means hostile and combative, not merely loud or excitable.
n.3: Fear could explain a refusal to leave, but belligerent means hostile and ready to fight.

VO.q: The dark, ominous clouds over the lake convinced the lifeguards to clear the beach early. Which word is closest in meaning to ominous as used in this sentence?
VO.w: The clouds made the lifeguards clear the beach, so they signaled danger. Ominous means threatening, suggesting that something bad is coming.

n.1: Scattered clouds would not usually clear a beach; ominous means threatening.
n.2: Low clouds may come with storms, but ominous is about a threat, not height.
n.3: Speed is a topic fit for storm clouds, but ominous describes a warning of harm, not motion.

VO.q: The baby was born at 34 weeks of gestation and needed help with feeding. What is the best definition of the word "gestation" in this sentence?
VO.w: Gestation is the period of development in the uterus: pregnancy.

n.0: Breaking down food is digestion, a look-alike word.
n.1: Labor is the birth process, the end of gestation.
n.2: Growth after birth is postnatal development, not gestation.

VO.q: Security camera footage helped corroborate the patient's account of how she fell in the parking lot. What is the best definition of the word corroborate in this sentence?
VO.w: Corroborate means to support or confirm with additional evidence.

n.0: Contradicting is the opposite of corroborating.
n.1: Cameras record, a topic fit, but corroborate means the footage supported her account.
n.2: Working together is collaborate, the look-alike.

VO.q: With the river still rising, flooding in the lower parking lot seemed inevitable to the hospital staff. What is the best definition of the word inevitable in this sentence?
VO.w: Inevitable means certain to happen; unavoidable.

n.0: Unnoticed describes awareness, not whether the flood will happen.
n.1: Unlikely is close to the opposite.
n.2: Floods are costly, a topic fit, but inevitable describes certainty.

VO.q: The team decided that home dialysis was feasible because the patient had a willing caregiver. What is the best definition of the word feasible in this sentence?
VO.w: Feasible means possible to do; practical.

n.0: Likely to fail is fallible, a look-alike.
n.1: Easy to bend is flexible, a look-alike.
n.3: Cost is a topic fit, but the caregiver made the plan possible; feasible means workable.

VO.q: Mrs. Owens chose to defer her knee surgery until after her daughter's wedding. What is the best definition of the word "defer" in this sentence?
VO.w: Defer means to put off until later; the word 'until' shows the surgery still happens.

n.0: Canceling ends the plan; deferring puts it off until later.
n.1: Referring sends a patient to someone else; it only sounds like defer.
n.3: Arranging the surgery is booking it, not delaying it.

VO.q: The medication can cause transient dizziness, so patients are told to rise slowly from bed. As used in this sentence, what does the word "transient" mean?
VO.w: Transient means lasting only a short time; passing.

n.0: Permanent is the opposite of transient.
n.2: Sudden and unexpected is abrupt; transient describes how long something lasts, not how it starts.
n.3: Frequent describes how often, not how long; transient means brief.

VO.q: The clinic offers a comprehensive eye exam for new patients on Saturday mornings. What is the best definition of the word comprehensive in this sentence?
VO.w: Comprehensive means including all or nearly all parts; complete.

n.1: Easy to understand is comprehensible, the look-alike.
n.2: Cost is a topic fit for a clinic offer, but comprehensive describes scope.
n.3: Quick and basic is the opposite of comprehensive.

VO.q: In the dim light, the nurse could barely discern the numbers printed on the small vial. What is the best definition of the word discern in this sentence?
VO.w: Discern means to notice or recognize, often with difficulty; to make out.

n.1: Throwing away is discard, a look-alike.
n.2: Worrying about something is concern, a look-alike.
n.3: Looking down on someone is disdain, another look-alike.

VO.q: A history of stomach bleeding is a contraindication for daily aspirin therapy. What is the best definition of the word "contraindication" in this sentence?
o: a reason to use a treatment
an unwanted effect of a drug
a new problem caused by a treatment
a reason not to use a treatment
VO.w: A contraindication is a condition that makes a treatment unsafe or inadvisable (contra- = against).

n.0: A reason to use a treatment is an indication, the opposite.
n.1: An unwanted effect is a side effect or adverse reaction.
n.2: A new problem arising during treatment is a complication.

VO.q: A mother brings her toddler to the clinic with a mild cold, a low fever, and persistent rhinorrhea. Based on its word parts, what is rhinorrhea?
VO.w: rhin/o means nose and -rrhea means flow or discharge, so rhinorrhea is a runny nose.

n.0: Inflammation of the nose is rhinitis (-itis).
n.2: Bleeding (bursting forth) is -rrhage or -rrhagia, the look-alike suffix.
n.3: Surgical repair is -plasty (rhinoplasty).

VO.q: Before the next patient's procedure, the technician cleaned and tested the endoscope according to the hospital's infection-control policy. Based on its suffix, what is an endoscope?
o: A record of images from inside the body
A surgical cut made into the body
A procedure that views inside the body
An instrument for viewing inside the body
VO.w: endo- means within and -scope means an instrument for viewing, so an endoscope is the instrument used to look inside the body.

n.0: A record or image is -gram; -scope is the viewing instrument.
n.1: A surgical cut is -otomy; nothing in endoscope refers to cutting.
n.2: The procedure is endoscopy; -scopy names the examination, while -scope names the instrument.

VO.q: Cold temperatures cause the blood vessels in the skin to constrict. What is the best definition of the word "constrict" in this sentence?
VO.w: Constrict means to make or become narrower.

n.1: Becoming wider is dilate, the opposite.
n.2: A blocked vessel is occluded; a constricted vessel is narrowed but still open.
n.3: Strength is not the meaning of constrict.

VO.q: Mr. Silva felt fine but was a carrier of the bacteria, so he stayed home from the food plant. As used in this sentence, what does the word "carrier" mean?
o: a person who is sick and infectious
a person immune to the germ
a healthy person who spreads germs
VO.w: A carrier harbors and can spread a pathogen without being ill.

n.0: A carrier is not ill; Mr. Silva felt fine.
n.1: Recovering means getting over an illness he never had.
n.2: An immune person is protected and does not harbor the germ.

VO.q: During a dressing change, the nurse documented a malodorous discharge from the patient's wound and notified the provider. Based on its prefix, what does malodorous mean?
VO.w: mal- means bad, and odor means smell, so malodorous means having a bad smell.

n.0: No smell would use a- or an- (without), not mal-.
n.1: Faint (less than normal) would match hypo-, not mal-.
n.3: A pleasant smell is the opposite of mal- (bad); good would be eu- or bene.

VO.q: The cyclist needed stitches for a laceration on her chin after she fell onto the gravel. As used in this sentence, what does the word "laceration" mean?
VO.w: A laceration is a torn or jagged cut in the skin, often closed with stitches.

n.0: A surface scrape is an abrasion; gravel makes this trap tempting, but scrapes rarely need stitches.
n.2: A bruise is a contusion; the skin is not broken.
n.3: A clean cut made with a blade on purpose is an incision.

VO.q: The first dose was given in the clinic, and subsequent doses will be taken at home. What is the best definition of the word subsequent in this sentence?
VO.w: Subsequent means coming after something else.

n.1: Dose size is a topic fit, but subsequent is about order in time.
n.2: Whether a dose is optional is a topic fit, but subsequent describes what comes next in time.
n.3: Earlier is the opposite (prior or preceding).

VO.q: The baby's birth appeared imminent, so the nurse moved Mrs. Ford to a delivery room. What is the best definition of the word "imminent" in this sentence?
VO.w: Imminent means about to happen very soon.

n.0: Protected from disease is immune.
n.2: Famous and respected is eminent, the classic sound-alike.
n.3: Overdue means late; imminent means about to occur.

VO.q: The pharmacy will issue a replacement inhaler as soon as the insurance approval arrives. What is the best definition of the word issue in this sentence?
VO.w: As a verb with an object (a replacement inhaler), issue means to give out or supply officially.

n.0: Looking into something treats issue as a problem to investigate (the noun sense); here the pharmacy hands over an inhaler.
n.2: Turning down is the opposite outcome; the pharmacy will supply the inhaler once approval arrives.
n.3: Payment is a topic fit with insurance, but issue means to give out, not to bill.

VO.q: Check the pulse distal to the bandage to be sure circulation is not blocked. What is the best definition of the word "distal" in this sentence?
VO.w: Distal means farther from the trunk or point of attachment, such as the wrist below an arm bandage.

n.0: The opposite side is contralateral.
n.2: Nearer the trunk is proximal, the opposite.
n.3: Under the bandage fits the sentence loosely, but distal describes distance from the trunk.

VO.q: The patient is receiving concurrent radiation and chemotherapy during the six-week program. What is the best definition of the word concurrent in this sentence?
VO.w: Concurrent means happening at the same time.

n.0: One after another is consecutive, the classic look-alike.
n.1: Current (up to date) shares letters but means something different.
n.2: Now and then is intermittent or sporadic, not at the same time.

VO.q: An interim manager will run the unit until a permanent replacement is hired this spring. What is the best definition of the word interim in this sentence?
VO.w: Interim means serving for the time between two events; temporary.

n.0: Inexperienced suggests intern, a look-alike.
n.1: Part-time describes hours worked; interim describes a limited period of service.
n.2: From inside suggests internal or interior, look-alikes.

VO.q: The cut on Owen's forearm was superficial, so the nurse closed it with adhesive strips. What is the best definition of the word "superficial" in this sentence?
VO.w: Superficial means near the surface; the opposite is deep.

n.0: A clean wound fits the sentence loosely, but superficial describes depth.
n.2: A jagged tear is a laceration; superficial says nothing about shape.
n.3: Higher on the body is superior, a look-alike word.

VO.q: During his lucid periods, Mr. Ellis recognized his daughter and talked about his garden. As used in this sentence, what does the word "lucid" mean?
VO.w: Lucid means clear-headed and able to think clearly.

n.0: Sleepy and dull is lethargic, nearly the opposite.
n.2: Calm, quiet periods fit the setting loosely, but lucid means clear-headed, not relaxed.
n.3: He did talk about his garden, but lucid describes clear thinking, not mood or talkativeness.

VO.q: Hospital policy proscribes the use of personal cell phones in the operating room. What is the best definition of the word "proscribe" in this sentence?
VO.w: Proscribe means to forbid or prohibit; prescribe means to order.

n.0: Describes only looks like proscribes.
n.2: Ordering is prescribe, the prescribe/proscribe sound-alike.
n.3: Permits is the opposite of proscribes.

VO.q: The nurse asked Mr. Reyes to void before she performed the bladder scan. What is the best definition of the word "void" in this sentence?
VO.w: In a patient sentence, void means to empty the bladder: to urinate.

n.0: Resting fits a pre-test instruction loosely, but void means to urinate.
n.2: Fasting is a different pre-test instruction.
n.3: Drinking fills the bladder; void means to empty it.

VO.q: The cream contains an ingredient that may inhibit the growth of new hair on treated skin. What is the best definition of the word inhibit in this sentence?
VO.w: Inhibit means to hold back or restrain; the ingredient slows hair growth.

n.0: Revealing or showing is exhibit, another look-alike.
n.1: Living in is inhabit, the look-alike word.
n.3: Speeding up is the opposite of inhibit (stimulate).

VO.q: After the anesthesia wore off, Mrs. Lin was alert and oriented when the nurse checked on her. What is the best definition of the word "oriented" in this sentence?
o: aware of self, place and time
able to move without any help
VO.w: Oriented means aware of who one is, where one is and the time.

n.0: Organized is a look-alike word.
n.2: Calm and rested fits recovery loosely, but oriented is about awareness.
n.3: Moving without help is ambulatory or independent.

VO.q: Three days after the fall, the bruise on her shin was still tender when the nurse pressed on it. What is the best definition of the word tender in this sentence?
VO.w: Tender has several senses; pressing on a bruise selects the sense "painful when touched."

n.0: Easy to chew is the food sense (tender meat); the sentence is about a bruise.
n.1: A bruise may be swollen, a topic fit, but tender here means painful when pressed, not swollen.
n.3: Gentle and loving is a real sense of tender (a tender smile), but a bruise that hurts when pressed rules it out.

VO.q: The resilient teenager returned to her soccer team only months after major knee surgery. What is the best definition of the word resilient in this sentence?
VO.w: Resilient means able to recover quickly from difficulty.

n.0: Resisting change is resistant, a look-alike.
n.2: Reluctant (unwilling) is a look-alike with the opposite sense here.
n.3: Eagerness to play is a topic fit for an athlete, but resilient means able to recover quickly, not keen to compete.

VO.q: The emergency department follows a strict protocol when a patient arrives with stroke symptoms. What is the best definition of the word "protocol" in this sentence?
VO.w: A protocol is an official, agreed set of steps for handling a situation, such as a suspected stroke.

n.0: An early model is a prototype, a look-alike word.
n.1: This fits the emergency setting loosely, but a protocol is a set of steps, not a group of people.
n.2: A single operation is a procedure; a protocol is the official plan of steps to follow.

VO.q: After the cardiac catheterization, Mr. Weiss must remain recumbent for four hours. What is the best definition of the word "recumbent" in this sentence?
VO.w: Recumbent means lying down.

n.0: Fasting fits a procedure loosely, but recumbent means lying down.
n.1: Sitting up is upright, the opposite of recumbent.
n.2: Alertness fits the recovery loosely, but recumbent describes position.

VO.q: The surgeon told Mr. Ortiz that the risk of infection from the procedure was negligible. What is the best definition of the word negligible in this sentence?
VO.w: Negligible means so small that it is unimportant.

n.0: Large and noticeable is the opposite (substantial).
n.1: Speed of onset is a topic fit for infection, but negligible is about size, not timing.
n.3: Caused by carelessness is the meaning of the look-alike negligent.

VO.q: Staff are trained to calm an argument in the waiting room before it can escalate. What is the best definition of the word escalate in this sentence?
VO.w: Escalate means to increase rapidly or become more intense.

n.1: Dying down is de-escalate, the opposite.
n.2: Beginning again is recur or restart; escalate means getting worse.
n.3: Reporting is a topic fit for a waiting-room incident, but escalate means to intensify.

VO.q: Mr. Patel's ankles showed edema by late afternoon, so he was told to raise his feet. What is the best definition of the word "edema" in this sentence?
VO.w: Edema is swelling caused by excess fluid in body tissues; raising the feet helps the fluid drain.

n.0: A scaly, itchy rash is eczema.
n.1: Stiff ankles fit the setting loosely, but edema is fluid swelling.
n.3: Redness is erythema, a look-alike word.

VO.q: The runner had an episode of syncope at the finish line and was carried to the medical tent. As used in this sentence, what does the word "syncope" mean?
VO.w: Syncope is fainting: a brief loss of consciousness from reduced blood flow to the brain.

n.1: A cramp fits a runner loosely, but syncope is loss of consciousness.
n.2: Shaking is a tremor or a seizure, not syncope.
n.3: A spinning sensation is vertigo.

VO.q: Dr. Lewis told the family that the boy's seizures were idiopathic. As used in this sentence, what does the word "idiopathic" mean?
VO.w: Idiopathic means arising from an unknown cause.

n.0: Caused by treatment is iatrogenic.
n.1: Passed down in families is hereditary.
n.3: Mental in origin is psychogenic; idiopathic says only that the cause is unknown.

VO.q: The X-ray showed no fracture, so the doctor described the injury to Ellie's shin as a contusion. As used in this sentence, what does the word "contusion" mean?
VO.w: A contusion is a bruise: bleeding under unbroken skin from a blow.

n.0: A sprain is a stretched or torn ligament at a joint.
n.1: A shallow scrape is an abrasion.
n.2: A hairline crack is a fracture, which the X-ray ruled out.

VO.q: When one kidney is removed, the other kidney often grows larger to compensate for the loss. What is the best definition of the word compensate in this sentence?
VO.w: Compensate (for) means to make up for a loss or lack.

n.0: Accounting for something means explaining it; the kidney grows to replace lost function, not to explain it.
n.1: Suffering from a loss is a topic fit, but the kidney's growth offsets the loss.
n.2: Preparing comes before an event; compensate responds to a loss that has already happened.

GR.q: Which sentence about the clinic staff uses correct subject-verb agreement?
o: Each of the new nurses have completed the orientation module.
Neither the manager nor the nurses was told about the fire drill.
The aides, together with the nurse, is checking the supply carts.
The staff meets in the conference room every Monday morning.
GR.w: "Staff" is a collective noun acting as one unit, so in US English it takes the singular verb "meets."

n.0: "Each" is singular, so the verb must be "has completed"; "nurses" sits in a prepositional phrase.
n.1: With "neither...nor," the verb agrees with the nearer subject, "nurses," so it must be "were told."
n.2: "Together with the nurse" does not change the subject; "aides" is plural, so the verb must be "are checking."

GR.q: Which sentence about a missed appointment is a comma splice?
o: The bus was late, we missed the appointment.
Because the bus was late, we missed the appointment.
The bus was late; we missed the appointment.
The bus was late, so we missed the appointment.
GR.w: A comma splice joins two independent clauses with only a comma. "The bus was late" and "we missed the appointment" can each stand alone.

n.1: The first clause is dependent (Because ...), so a comma after it is correct.
n.2: A semicolon correctly joins two independent clauses.
n.3: A comma plus the coordinating conjunction "so" correctly joins two independent clauses.

GR.q: Which word in the sentence has an unclear antecedent? "When Ella handed Dana the report, which had just arrived, she noticed that its last page was missing."
GR.w: "She" could mean Ella or Dana, so its antecedent is unclear. "Which" and "its" can refer only to the report.

n.1: "Its" can refer only to the report, the one thing in the sentence that has pages.
n.2: "That" after "noticed" is a conjunction introducing a clause, not a pronoun, so it has no antecedent.
n.3: "Which" comes right after "the report" and can refer only to it.

GR.q: In the sentence "Everyone in the waiting room heard the announcement," what part of speech is the word "Everyone"?
GR.w: "Everyone" is an indefinite pronoun: it stands in for people without naming them.

n.0: An adjective describes a noun; "Everyone" is the subject of "heard."
n.1: A noun names a person, place, thing or idea; "Everyone" refers to people without naming any of them.
n.2: An adverb modifies a verb, adjective or adverb; "Everyone" is the subject.

GR.q: Which sentence uses a possessive pronoun correctly?
o: Is the stethoscope on the counter your's?
The blue lunch bag on the top shelf is her's.
The final decision about surgery was theirs.
The clinic updated it's visiting hours today.
GR.w: Possessive pronouns (hers, theirs, its, yours) take no apostrophe, so "theirs" is correct.

n.0: "Your's" is not a standard form; the possessive pronoun is "yours."
n.1: "Her's" is not a standard form; the possessive pronoun is "hers."
n.3: "It's" means "it is"; the possessive is "its": "updated its visiting hours."

GR.q: Which sentence contains a shift in pronoun person that should be corrected?
o: When one reads a drug label, you should check the expiration date first.
If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember it.
We volunteers should bring our badges to every shift this month.
Applicants should check their email often, since the school sends updates there.
GR.w: "One" is third person, but "you" is second person. Keep one point of view: "When you read a drug label, you should..."

n.1: This sentence stays in second person throughout ("you" and the implied "you" of "take").
n.2: This sentence stays in first person plural: "we" and "our."
n.3: This sentence is consistent: "applicants" and "their" are both third person plural.

GR.q: Which sentence uses "than" and "then" correctly?
o: The test took longer then expected, so we ate lunch and than left.
The test took longer than expected, so we ate lunch and than left.
The test took longer then expected, so we ate lunch and then left.
The test took longer than expected, so we ate lunch and then left.
GR.w: "Than" makes a comparison (longer than expected); "then" shows time or sequence (and then left).

n.0: Both are reversed: the comparison needs "than" and the sequence needs "then".
n.1: "And ___ left" shows sequence, so it needs "then".
n.2: "Longer ___ expected" is a comparison, so it needs "than".

GR.q: Which sentence avoids a vague pronoun reference?
o: The employee handbook states that meal breaks last thirty minutes.
The handbook and the shift schedule both list breaks, and it says they last thirty minutes.
They say in the employee handbook that meal breaks last thirty minutes.
In the employee handbook, they state that meal breaks last thirty minutes.
GR.w: Every pronoun needs a clear antecedent. Making "the employee handbook" the subject removes the vague "they" or "it."

n.1: "It" could mean the handbook or the shift schedule, so the reference is unclear even though both nouns are named.
n.2: "They" has no antecedent; the sentence never names who "they" are.
n.3: "They" is vague: the handbook is a thing, and no people have been named.

GR.q: Which sentence from a hospital welcome packet contains an error in subject-verb agreement?
o: Neither of the two applicants has submitted a transcript yet.
The bag of IV fluid hanging by the bed is due to be replaced.
There are a clipboard and two pens at the front desk for visitors.
Each of the patients on the third floor have a call button.
GR.w: "Each" is always singular, so the verb must be "has": "Each of the patients on the third floor has a call button." The plural "patients" sits inside a prepositional phrase.

n.0: This sentence is correct: "neither" used as a pronoun is singular, so "has submitted" agrees.
n.1: This sentence is correct: the subject "bag" is singular and takes "is"; "of IV fluid hanging by the bed" does not change it.
n.2: This sentence is correct: the subject after the verb is compound ("a clipboard and two pens"), so the plural "are" agrees.

GR.q: Which sentence from an end-of-day inventory report uses correct subject-verb agreement?
o: Some of the patients in the waiting room is asking about the delay.
Most of the hand sanitizer in the supply room has been used this week.
All of the lab samples from this morning has been labeled and stored.
Half of the coffee in the break room were gone by the end of the night shift.
GR.w: All, some, most and fractions such as half take their number from the noun after "of." "Sanitizer" is uncountable, so "Most of the hand sanitizer ... has been used" is correct.

n.0: "Some" refers to "patients" (plural) here, so the verb must be "are asking."
n.2: "All" takes its number from the noun after "of." "Samples" is plural, so the verb must be "have been labeled."
n.3: "Half" agrees with the noun after "of." "Coffee" is uncountable, so the verb must be singular: "was gone."

GR.q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "The new meal plan calls for ___ sodium and ___ processed snacks each day."
GR.w: Sodium is uncountable, so "less sodium"; snacks can be counted, so "fewer processed snacks."

n.0: Sodium cannot be counted one by one, so it takes "less," not "fewer."
n.1: Both are reversed: uncountable sodium takes "less," and countable snacks take "fewer."
n.3: "Snacks" is a countable plural, so it takes "fewer," not "less."

GR.q: In the sentence "The nurse gently lifted the crying toddler onto the exam table," what part of speech is the word "crying"?
GR.w: "Crying" tells which toddler (the one who is crying), so this -ing form is a participle acting as an adjective that describes the noun "toddler."

n.0: An adverb would tell how the nurse lifted; "gently" does that job, while "crying" modifies the noun "toddler."
n.1: "Crying" has no helping verb (is, was), so it is not a verb here; the only verb in the sentence is "lifted."
n.3: An -ing form is a noun (a gerund) when it names an activity ("Crying tires a child"); here it describes "toddler."

GR.q: The flyers have large print. Which sentence places the modifier "with large print" correctly?
o: The volunteer handed out flyers to the families with large print.
The volunteer handed out flyers with large print to the families.
The volunteer with large print handed out flyers to the families.
With large print, the volunteer handed out flyers to the families.
GR.w: A modifier belongs next to the word it describes. The large print is on the flyers, so the phrase must follow "flyers."

n.0: Placed after "families," the phrase seems to describe the families, not the flyers.
n.2: Placed after "volunteer," the phrase describes the volunteer instead of the flyers.
n.3: Placed at the start, the phrase seems to describe the volunteer, who is not printed.

GR.q: Read the sentence: "When the doctor enters the room, the patient sat up in bed." Which revision corrects the tense error?
GR.w: Both actions happen in the same time frame. Matching "sat" to the present "enters" gives "When the doctor enters the room, the patient sits up in bed."

n.1: English uses the present tense, not "will," after "when" in a time clause, and the clash with "sat" would remain.
n.2: "Has sat" is the present perfect, a finished action, which still does not match the habit shown by "enters."
n.3: "Sitting" without a helping verb cannot be the main verb, so the main clause would have no complete verb.

GR.q: Which revision corrects the pronoun shift in "When a nurse starts on a new unit, you should ask for a tour"?
o: When nurses start on a new unit, she should ask for a tour.
When nurses start on a new unit, they should ask for a tour.
When nurses start on a new unit, you should ask for a tour.
When a nurse starts on a new unit, we should ask for a tour.
GR.w: "Nurses" (third person plural) is matched by "they" (third person plural), so person and number agree.

n.0: "She" is singular, but the antecedent "nurses" is plural.
n.2: This still shifts from third person ("nurses") to second person ("you").
n.3: This shifts from third person ("a nurse") to first person ("we").

GR.q: Which revision corrects the faulty parallelism in "The new policy is meant to reduce wait times, improving patient satisfaction, and to lower costs"?
GR.w: Two of the three items are infinitives (to reduce, to lower). Changing "improving" to "to improve" makes all three match.

n.0: This leaves "to lower" as an infinitive while the other two items are gerunds, so the list is still mixed.
n.1: This leaves "to reduce" as an infinitive while the other two items are gerunds, so the list is still mixed.
n.2: Removing "and" does not change the forms of the items and also leaves the series without its conjunction.

GR.q: Which sentence uses a comparative or superlative form correctly?
o: Of the two inhalers, the blue one is the most effective for her asthma.
Of the three textbooks, this one is the better choice for anatomy.
The night shift is more busier than the day shift on most weekends.
Of the three dressings, the foam one is the least painful to remove.
GR.w: With three or more items, use the superlative (-est, most, least). Three dressings are compared, so "least painful" is correct.
