n.0: Comparing exactly two items calls for the comparative: "the more effective."
n.1: Comparing three or more items calls for the superlative: "the best choice."
n.2: "More busier" is a double comparative; use "busier" alone.

GR.q: Read the sentence: "Since the new reminder policy started, the clinic has saw fewer missed appointments." Which revision corrects the verb error?
GR.w: Two steps: "since" calls for the present perfect, and a singular subject ("clinic") takes "has" + the past participle "seen."

n.0: "Saw" is the simple past and cannot follow any helping verb; the participle is "seen."
n.1: "Seen" is right, but "clinic" is singular, so the helping verb must stay "has."
n.2: A past participle cannot stand alone as the main verb; it needs "has."

GR.q: Which word in the sentence is used incorrectly? "The pharmacy and the lab will extend it's hours during the flu season."
GR.w: The antecedent "the pharmacy and the lab" is plural, so the pronoun must be "their." "It's" also means "it is," not a possessive.

n.1: "During" is a correct preposition before "the flu season."
n.2: "Will extend" is a correct future verb for the plural subject.
n.3: "Pharmacy" is correct as part of the compound subject.

GR.q: Which sentence uses the correct past or past participle form?
o: The volunteer brung extra blankets to the shelter.
The phone rang twice before the nurse answered it.
The bell had rang twice before the class started.
The toddler had tore the paper gown into pieces.
GR.w: "Rang" is the simple past of "ring" and stands alone without a helping verb.

n.0: "Brung" is nonstandard; the past of "bring" is "brought."
n.2: After "had," the past participle "rung" is needed: "had rung."
n.3: After "had," the past participle "torn" is needed: "had torn."

GR.q: In the sentence "The patient has been resting quietly since noon," which word is the main verb?
GR.w: In the verb phrase "has been resting," "has" and "been" are helping verbs; "resting" carries the main action.

n.0: "Been" is a helping verb here; it supports "resting."
n.1: "Has" is a helping verb that forms the perfect tense.
n.3: "Quietly" is an adverb telling how the patient was resting.

GR.q: Which sentence for a clinic's front-desk sign uses possessive pronouns correctly?
o: The clinic updated its' hours, and the new schedule is yours.
The clinic updated it's hours, and the new schedule is yours.
The clinic updated its hours, and the new schedule is yours.
The clinic updated its hours, and the new schedule is your's.
GR.w: Possessive pronouns (its, yours, hers, ours, theirs, whose) never take an apostrophe.

n.0: "Its'" is not a word; the possessive pronoun is "its".
n.1: "It's" means "it is" or "it has"; the possessive is "its".
n.3: "Yours" is a possessive pronoun and takes no apostrophe.

GR.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? "Before the exam began, Ms. Ruiz ___ her photo ID on the proctor's desk."
GR.w: Putting the ID down takes an object ("her photo ID"), so the verb is "lay," and its simple past is "laid."

n.0: "Layed" is not a standard form; the past of "lay" is "laid."
n.1: "Lay" here would be the past of "lie" (to recline), which takes no object.
n.2: "Lain" is the past participle of "lie" and needs a helping verb.

GR.q: Which version of a quotation split by a dialogue tag is punctuated correctly?
o: "I can't stay," Leah said. "because my shift starts at noon."
"I can't stay," Leah said, "because my shift starts at noon."
"I can't stay," Leah said, "Because my shift starts at noon."
"I can't stay", Leah said, "because my shift starts at noon."
GR.w: Two steps: the quotation is one sentence interrupted by the tag, so a comma follows the tag and the second part continues in lowercase. In US style the comma after "stay" goes inside the quotation mark.

n.0: A period after "said" would start a new sentence, which would need a capital; but "because ..." continues the first sentence, so a comma is needed.
n.2: The second part continues the same sentence, so "because" is not capitalized.
n.3: In US style the comma goes inside the closing quotation mark.

GR.q: Which revision of "When one starts a new job, you often feel nervous" corrects the shift in person?
o: When one starts a new job, we often feel nervous.
When you start a new job, you often feel nervous.
When you start a new job, one often feels nervous.
When one starts a new job, I often feel nervous.
GR.w: "You ... you" keeps the same (second) person throughout. ("One ... one" would also be consistent.)

n.0: The sentence shifts from third person ("one") to first person ("we").
n.2: The shift is reversed: second person ("you") to third person ("one").
n.3: The sentence shifts from third person ("one") to first person ("I").

GR.q: Which sentence about Riverside Clinic is punctuated correctly?
o: Riverside Clinic, which opened in 2020, now offers evening hours.
Riverside Clinic, which opened in 2020 now offers evening hours.
Riverside Clinic which opened in 2020, now offers evening hours.
Riverside Clinic which opened in 2020 now offers evening hours.
GR.w: A proper noun is already identified, so the clause "which opened in 2020" is nonessential and needs a pair of commas.

n.1: The closing comma after "2020" is missing.
n.2: The opening comma after "Riverside Clinic" is missing.
n.3: A nonessential clause after a proper noun must be set off with commas.

GR.q: In the sentence "The nurse placed a warm blanket over the shivering patient," what part of speech is the word "over"?
GR.w: "Over" links its object, "the shivering patient," to the verb "placed," showing where the blanket went, so it is a preposition.

n.0: "Over" would be an adverb only with no object after it ("The aide came over"); here it has the object "patient."
n.1: "Shivering" is the adjective describing "patient"; "over" shows a relationship of place.
n.3: A conjunction joins words or clauses; "over" introduces a noun phrase, not a clause.

GR.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? "The guest speaker has ___ about patient safety at every orientation since 2022."
GR.w: Speak, spoke, spoken: after "has," use the past participle "spoken."

n.0: "Spoke" is the simple past and cannot follow "has."
n.2: "Speak" is irregular; "speaked" is not a standard form.
n.3: "Speak" is the base form and cannot follow "has."

GR.q: In the sentence "The nurse felt the patient's forehead for a fever," what kind of verb is "felt"?
GR.w: The nurse performed an action on an object (the forehead), so "felt" is an action verb here.

n.0: An infinitive is "to" plus a verb ("to feel").
n.2: A helping verb supports a main verb ("has felt"); "felt" is the only verb.
n.3: "Felt" is a linking verb when a description of the subject follows ("The nurse felt tired"); here it has an object.

GR.q: Which sentence uses adjectives and adverbs correctly?
o: The team did good on the state safety inspection this year.
The new graduate handled the emergency calm and careful.
After a night of rest, Jordan felt well enough to go to class.
The cafeteria soup tasted differently after the new cook started.
GR.w: "Well" can be an adjective meaning "in good health," so "felt well" is correct after the linking verb "felt."

n.0: "Did" is an action verb here, so it needs the adverb "well": "did well on the inspection."
n.1: "Calm" and "careful" describe how she handled it, so they modify a verb and must be adverbs: "calmly and carefully."
n.3: "Tasted" is a linking verb here, so it takes an adjective that describes the soup: "tasted different."

GR.q: Which sentence using "however" contains a comma error?
o: However, the results were not available until Tuesday.
The results were not available until Tuesday, however.
The results were not available, however until Tuesday.
The results, however, were not available until Tuesday.
GR.w: "However" used as an interrupter in the middle of a clause must be set off by commas on both sides: "available, however, until Tuesday". One comma is missing.

n.0: Correct: an introductory "However" is followed by a comma.
n.1: Correct: a closing "however" is preceded by a comma.
n.3: Correct: the interrupter is enclosed by a pair of commas.

GR.q: Which sentence from a shift report is punctuated correctly?
o: The nurse, checked the patient's chart and the doctor reviewed the latest lab results.
The nurse checked the patient's chart, and, the doctor reviewed the latest lab results.
The nurse checked the patient's chart, and the doctor reviewed the latest lab results.
The nurse checked the patient's chart and, the doctor reviewed the latest lab results.
GR.w: When a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) joins two independent clauses, a comma goes before the conjunction: "chart, and the doctor".

n.0: A comma must not separate a subject (The nurse) from its verb (checked), and the comma before "and" is missing.
n.1: No comma follows a coordinating conjunction; only the comma before "and" is needed.
n.3: The comma belongs before the conjunction, not after it.

GR.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? "Mr. Diaz has been a patient on the cardiac unit ___ Monday."
GR.w: "Since" marks the starting point of a period that continues to now: since Monday.

n.0: "From" needs an end point (from Monday until Friday) and does not fit "has been."
n.1: "For" is used with a length of time (for three days), not a starting day.
n.2: "Until" marks an end point (until Monday), but "has been" needs the starting point.

GR.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? "Patients should abstain ___ food and drink for eight hours before the test."
GR.w: The standard idiom is "abstain from."

n.1: "Abstain of" is nonstandard; the verb takes "from."
n.2: "Abstain to" is nonstandard; the verb takes "from."
n.3: "Abstain with" is nonstandard; the verb takes "from."

GR.q: Which sentence confirming a patient's paperwork is punctuated correctly?
o: Ms. Chen, you finished, the intake form didn't you?
Ms. Chen, you finished the intake form, didn't you?
Ms. Chen, you finished the intake form didn't you?
Ms. Chen you finished the intake form, didn't you?
GR.w: A name in direct address is set off by a comma, and a tag question (didn't you?) is also set off by a comma.

n.0: A comma must not separate the verb (finished) from its object, and the comma before the tag question is missing.
n.2: The comma before the tag question "didn't you" is missing.
n.3: The comma after the name in direct address is missing.

GR.q: Which revision corrects the dangling modifier in "After reviewing the lab results, a new medication was ordered"?
o: After reviewing the lab results, the doctor ordered a new medication.
After reviewing the lab results, the doctor's order called for a new medication.
After reviewing the lab results, a new medication was ordered by the doctor.
After reviewing the lab results, the doctor's decision was to order a new medication.
GR.w: The person who reviewed the results (the doctor) must be the subject right after the introductory phrase.

n.1: The subject after the comma is "order," so the sentence says the order reviewed the results; the doctor must be the subject.
n.2: The subject after the comma is still "a new medication," so the sentence still says the medication reviewed the results.
n.3: The subject after the comma is "decision," and a decision cannot review lab results; "doctor's" is only a possessive.

GR.q: Which sentence from a vaccination schedule is capitalized correctly?
o: We hold the flu clinic every fall, starting the Monday after labor day.
We hold the flu clinic every fall, starting the Monday after Labor Day.
We hold the flu clinic every Fall, starting the Monday after Labor Day.
We hold the flu clinic every fall, starting the monday after Labor Day.
GR.w: Days of the week and holidays are proper nouns (Monday, Labor Day), but seasons are not capitalized unless they are part of a name.

n.0: The name of a holiday is a proper noun, so "Labor Day" is capitalized.
n.2: Seasons such as fall are common nouns and are not capitalized.
n.3: Days of the week are proper nouns, so "Monday" is capitalized.

GR.q: In the sentence "The infection cleared, but the cough lingered for two more weeks," what part of speech is the word "but"?
GR.w: "But" joins two independent clauses ("The infection cleared" and "the cough lingered"), so it is a coordinating conjunction.

n.0: An interjection stands apart to show feeling; "but" connects the two halves of the sentence.
n.2: An adverb modifies a verb, adjective or adverb; "but" links two complete thoughts.
n.3: "But" is a preposition only when it means "except" and takes an object ("everyone but Sam"); here it joins two clauses.

GR.q: Which sentence from a lab update is punctuated correctly?
o: The lab closed early the samples will be tested tomorrow.
Because the lab closed early; the samples will be tested tomorrow.
The lab closed early; the samples will be tested tomorrow.
The lab closed early, the samples will be tested tomorrow.
GR.w: A semicolon can join two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction.

n.0: Two independent clauses with no punctuation between them form a run-on (fused) sentence.
n.1: "Because the lab closed early" is a dependent clause; a semicolon must join two independent clauses, so a comma belongs here.
n.3: Joining two independent clauses with only a comma creates a comma splice.

GR.q: Which sentence from a new graduate's cover letter is capitalized correctly?
o: After moving to the Midwest, she drove South to visit her family.
After moving to the midwest, she drove South to visit her family.
After moving to the Midwest, she drove south to visit her family.
After moving to the midwest, she drove south to visit her family.
GR.w: A compass word is capitalized when it names a region (the Midwest) but not when it gives a direction (drove south).

n.0: "Drove south" gives a direction, not a region, so it is lowercase.
n.1: Both are reversed: the region is capitalized and the direction is lowercase.
n.3: "The Midwest" names a region of the country, so it is capitalized.

GR.q: Which sentence uses "good" or "well" correctly?
o: The team performed good during the mock code drill.
Ms. Dorsey sang well at the hospital fundraiser.
The incision is healing good, so the stitches can come out.
The new monitor works good once it is calibrated.
GR.w: "Sang" is an action verb, so it takes the adverb "well."

n.0: "Performed" is an action verb and needs the adverb "well."
n.2: "Healing" is an action and needs the adverb "well": "is healing well."
n.3: "Works" is an action verb and needs the adverb "well": "works well."

GR.q: Which sentence quoting a board member's comment is punctuated correctly?
o: She called the plan "a good start," the board disagreed.
She called the plan "a good start"; the board disagreed.
She called the plan, "a good start"; the board disagreed.
She called the plan "a good start;" the board disagreed.
GR.w: In US style, semicolons and colons go outside the closing quotation mark (only periods and commas go inside).

n.0: A comma alone between two independent clauses creates a comma splice.
n.2: The quoted words are part of the sentence's structure (the plan is called something), so no comma should introduce them.
n.3: A semicolon goes outside the closing quotation mark.

GR.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? "By the time the night shift began, the moon had already ___."
GR.w: The moon goes up by itself (no object), so the verb is "rise": rise, rose, risen. After "had," use "risen."

n.0: "Rise" is irregular; "rised" is not a standard form.
n.2: "Rose" is the simple past and cannot follow "had."
n.3: "Raised" is a form of "raise," which needs an object (raise something).

GR.q: Which sentence repeating a doctor's instruction is punctuated correctly?
o: Did the doctor really say "no visitors."
Did the doctor really say "no visitors?"
Did the doctor really say "no visitors".
Did the doctor really say "no visitors"?
GR.w: The whole sentence is a question, but the quoted words are not. A question mark that belongs to the whole sentence goes outside the closing quotation mark.

n.0: The sentence is a direct question, so it must end with a question mark.
n.1: The quoted words "no visitors" are not a question, so the question mark does not belong inside the quotation marks.
n.2: The sentence is a direct question, so it must end with a question mark, not a period.

GR.q: Which sentence from a weekly staffing update is structured correctly?
o: The clinic was short-staffed on Friday. Because several walk-ins arrived before nine.
Although the clinic was short-staffed, the nurses kept every visit on schedule.
The clinic was short-staffed on Friday, several walk-in patients arrived before nine.
The clinic was short-staffed on Friday several walk-in patients arrived before nine.
GR.w: A dependent clause (Although the clinic was short-staffed) followed by a comma and an independent clause is a correct complex sentence.

n.0: The second word group begins with "Because" and has no independent clause, so it is a fragment.
n.2: Two independent clauses joined by only a comma form a comma splice.
n.3: Two independent clauses with no punctuation or conjunction form a run-on (fused) sentence.

GR.q: A writer quotes "The vaccine, which was tested for two years, is safe for adults" but leaves out the middle clause. Which mark shows where words were removed?
GR.w: An ellipsis (three periods) shows that words have been left out of a quotation: "The vaccine ... is safe for adults."

n.1: Parentheses enclose extra information; they do not show an omission.
n.2: Brackets mark words the writer adds to a quotation, not words taken out.
n.3: A dash marks a sudden break or adds emphasis; it does not show an omission.

GR.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? "The results of the patient's blood test ___ ready for the cardiologist to review."
GR.w: The subject is "results," which is plural, so the verb is "are." "Of the patient's blood test" is an intervening prepositional phrase.

n.0: "Is" agrees with "test," the object of the preposition, not with the plural subject "results."
n.2: "Was" is singular; the plural subject "results" needs "are" (or "were").
n.3: "Has been" is singular; the plural subject "results" would need "have been."

GR.q: Which sentence from a lab safety notice uses a pronoun that agrees with its antecedent?
o: Each of the vials must be inspected for cracks before it is used.
The lab and the pharmacy will extend its hours in December.
If a student wants to pass, you have to practice every day.
All of the incubators must have its filters changed every month.
GR.w: "Each" is singular, and a vial is a thing, so the singular pronoun "it" agrees in number and person.

n.1: Two antecedents joined by "and" are plural, so the pronoun must be "their hours."
n.2: The sentence shifts from third person ("a student") to second person ("you"); keep the same person throughout.
n.3: "All" refers to "incubators" (plural) here, so the pronoun must be plural: "their filters."

GR.q: Which sentence about flu season uses prepositions of time correctly?
o: Flu shots start on October and end in early March.
Flu shots start in October and end in early March.
Flu shots start at October and end on early March.
Flu shots start in October and end at early March.
GR.w: Months and parts of a month take "in": in October, in early March.

n.0: "On" is for days and dates; a month takes "in."
n.2: "At" is for clock times and "on" for days; months take "in."
n.3: "At" is for clock times; "early March" is part of a month and takes "in."

GR.q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "The counselor's open questions helped ___ honest answers about the teen's ___ drug use."
GR.w: "Elicit" is a verb meaning to draw out; "illicit" is an adjective meaning illegal.

n.0: After "helped," a verb meaning to draw out is needed: "elicit."
n.2: An adjective meaning illegal is needed before "drug use": "illicit."
n.3: Both are reversed: "helped ___ answers" needs the verb "elicit," and illegal drug use is "illicit."

GR.q: Which sentence about a pediatric patient uses hyphens correctly?
o: The two-year-old girl is in Room 4, and her brother is five-years-old.
The two-year-old girl is in Room 4, and her brother is five years old.
The two-year old girl is in Room 4, and her brother is five years old.
The two year old girl is in Room 4, and her brother is five years old.
GR.w: A compound modifier before a noun takes hyphens (a two-year-old girl), but the same words after the noun do not (five years old).

n.0: "Five years old" follows the verb, not a noun, so it takes no hyphens.
n.2: Every word of the compound modifier is joined: "two-year-old," not "two-year old."
n.3: "Two-year-old" comes before the noun "girl," so it needs hyphens.

GR.q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "The school's ____ explained that honesty is a basic ____ of the honor code."
GR.w: "Principal" names the head of a school (or means "main"); "principle" is a rule or belief, as in a principle of the honor code.

n.0: A basic rule of a code is a "principle", not a "principal".
n.2: The head of a school is the "principal", not a "principle".
n.3: Both words are reversed: the school's head is the principal, and a rule is a principle.

GR.q: Which word in the sentence is used incorrectly? "Because the clinic has opened its second office, Dr. Liu and myself will divide our hours between the two sites."
GR.w: "Dr. Liu and ___" is the subject of "will divide," so it needs the subjective "I": "Dr. Liu and I will divide our hours." "Myself" has no "I" earlier in the sentence to reflect.

n.0: "Our" correctly refers to Dr. Liu and the speaker together.
n.2: "Its" is the correct possessive for one clinic, written without an apostrophe.
n.3: "Between" is correct with two sites, and its object is a noun, not a pronoun.

GR.q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "A large ___ of visitors left a surprising ___ of trash in the lobby."
GR.w: Visitors can be counted ("number of visitors"); trash cannot ("amount of trash").

n.0: Both are reversed: countable visitors take "number," and uncountable trash takes "amount."
n.2: Visitors are countable, so they take "number," not "amount."
n.3: Trash is uncountable, so it takes "amount," not "number."

GR.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? "The nurse spoke ___ to the frightened child before the blood draw."
GR.w: "Spoke" is an action verb, so the word that tells how she spoke must be an adverb: "gently."

n.0: "Gentle" is an adjective; it can describe a person or a touch but not the action "spoke."
n.1: "Gentlest" is a superlative adjective, and nothing is being compared or described.
n.2: "Gentleness" is a noun; it would need "with" before it ("spoke with gentleness").

MA.q: At a clinic, the ratio of new patients to returning patients is 5:7. If 35 new patients came on Monday, how many more returning patients than new patients came?
MA.w: One part = 35 ÷ 5 = 7 patients. Returning patients = 7 × 7 = 49. Difference: 49 - 35 = 14.

n.0: This is the number of returning patients, not how many more returning patients there were.
n.2: This finds 2/7 of 35, dividing by the returning term (7) instead of the new term (5) to get one part.
n.3: This subtracts the ratio terms (7 - 5). Each part stands for 7 patients, so the difference is 2 × 7 = 14.

MA.q: A bag holds 1 1/2 cups of rice. A cook uses 3/4 cup, and then uses 2/3 of the rice that remains. How many cups of rice does the cook use in the second step?
MA.w: Remaining after the first step: 1 1/2 - 3/4 = 6/4 - 3/4 = 3/4 cup. Second step: 2/3 × 3/4 = 6/12 = 1/2 cup.

n.0: 3/4 cup is what remains after the first step, before the 2/3 is taken.
n.1: 1/4 cup is what is left in the bag after both steps.
n.2: 1 1/8 divides 3/4 by 2/3 instead of multiplying (taking 2/3 of an amount means multiply).

MA.q: A 120 mL bottle of liquid medication contains 250 mg per 5 mL. The dose is 500 mg twice a day. How many full days will the bottle last?
MA.w: One dose: 500 ÷ 250 × 5 = 10 mL. Per day: 2 × 10 = 20 mL. Days: 120 ÷ 20 = 6 days.

n.0: This uses desired ÷ have (2) as the dose in mL, giving 4 mL per day.
n.1: This is the number of doses (120 ÷ 10), not days; there are 2 doses a day.
n.3: This inverts the ratio, giving 2.5 mL per dose and 5 mL per day.

MA.q: A cell-culture protocol calls for 0.075 L of buffer solution. The graduated cylinder on the bench is marked in milliliters. Enter the volume to measure, in milliliters, as a whole number.

tr.750: Moved the decimal point four places.
tr.7.5: Moved the decimal point only two places (multiplied by 100, the centi factor).
tr.0.000075: Divided by 1,000 instead of multiplying when going from a larger to a smaller unit.

MA.w: 1 L = 1,000 mL. Converting from a larger unit (liters) to a smaller unit (milliliters) means multiplying: 0.075 x 1,000 = 75 mL. Move the decimal point three places to the right.

MA.q: A patient's height is recorded as 165.1 cm. What is the patient's height in feet and inches?

n.0: This turns 65 in into 5.42 ft and reads the decimal .4 as 4 inches; the remainder is 5 in.
n.1: This splits 65 inches as if a foot were 10 inches; 1 ft = 12 in.
n.2: This rounds the factor to 2.5 (165.1 ÷ 2.5 = 66 in); the exact factor is 2.54.

MA.q: A bottle contains 15 tablets. Each prescribed dose is 3/4 of a tablet, and tablets are scored so they can be split. How many doses does the bottle contain?
MA.w: Divide the supply by the dose: 15 ÷ 3/4 = 15 × 4/3 = 60/3 = 20 doses.

n.0: 11 1/4 is 15 × 3/4, the multiplication instead of the division.
n.2: 5 divides 15 by the numerator 3 and ignores the denominator 4.
n.3: 60 multiplies by 4 but does not then divide by 3.

MA.q: Four students each completed part of the same online module. The parts completed were 5/9, 4/7, 6/11 and 7/13. Which fraction of the module is greatest?
MA.w: Convert to decimals: 4/7 ≈ 0.571, 5/9 ≈ 0.556, 6/11 ≈ 0.545, 7/13 ≈ 0.538. The greatest is 4/7. (Cross-multiplying 4/7 and 5/9 also works: 4 × 9 = 36 > 5 × 7 = 35.)

n.0: 5/9 ≈ 0.556, slightly less than 4/7 ≈ 0.571 (cross products 35 < 36).
n.1: 7/13 ≈ 0.538 is actually the least; a larger denominator does not mean a larger fraction.
n.2: 6/11 ≈ 0.545; its larger numerator and denominator do not make it larger.

MA.w: Line up the points: 14.700 + 3.080 + 0.256. Thousandths 6; hundredths 8 + 5 = 13, write 3, carry 1; tenths 7 + 2 + 1 = 10, write 0, carry 1; ones 4 + 3 + 1 = 8; tens 1. Total 18.036.

n.0: 17.936 forgets the 1 carried from the hundredths column into the tenths.
n.2: 17.036 forgets the 1 carried from the tenths column into the ones.
n.3: 20.34 reads 0.256 as 2.56, shifting its digits one place left.

MA.q: A long division has a divisor of 13, a quotient of 47 and a remainder of 9. What is the dividend?
MA.w: Dividend = quotient × divisor + remainder = 47 × 13 + 9 = 611 + 9 = 620. Check: 620 ÷ 13 = 47 R 9.

n.1: 611 is quotient × divisor but leaves out the remainder of 9.
n.2: 602 subtracts the remainder from 611 instead of adding it; the remainder is added back to quotient × divisor.
n.3: 600 drops the carried 2 in 47 × 3 (121 instead of 141), so 47 × 13 comes out as 591 before the 9 is added.

MA.w: Parentheses: 3 - 7 = -4. Multiply: -2 × (-4) = 8. Subtracting a negative is adding: 8 - (-5) = 8 + 5 = 13.

n.0: 3 treats - (-5) as -5 instead of +5 (8 - 5).
n.1: -8 distributes -2 to the 3 only: -6 - 7 + 5.
n.2: -3 gives -2 × (-4) a negative sign (-8 + 5); the product of two negatives is positive.

MA.q: A hospital cafeteria needs 12 gallons of soup for a staff event. The soup comes in 4-liter containers. Use 1 liter = 1.06 quarts. What is the least number of containers the cafeteria must order?
MA.w: 12 gal × 4 = 48 qt. 48 ÷ 1.06 = 45.28 L. 45.28 ÷ 4 = 11.32, so round up to 12 containers.

n.1: This does not convert gallons to quarts (12 ÷ 1.06 = 11.3 L, then 11.3 ÷ 4 = 2.8); 1 gal = 4 qt.
n.2: 45.28 L ÷ 4 = 11.3, and 11 containers fall short, so round up.
n.3: This multiplies 48 qt by 1.06 (50.88) instead of dividing, then divides by 4 to get 12.7.

MA.q: A hospital's 30-day readmission rate dropped from 16% to 12% after a new discharge program. By what percent did the readmission rate decrease?
MA.w: The rate fell 16 - 12 = 4 percentage points. Percent decrease = 4 ÷ 16 × 100 = 25%.

n.0: This is the change in percentage points (16 - 12), not the percent decrease.
n.1: This divides the 4-point change by the new rate, 12%, instead of the original rate, 16%.
n.2: This is the new rate as a percent of the old rate, 12 ÷ 16.

MA.q: A unit has a $1,200 equipment budget. It spends 40% on monitors and then 25% of the remaining money on supplies. How much of the budget is left?

n.1: $720 is the amount left after the monitors, one step short of the answer.
n.2: $420 adds the percents (40% + 25% = 65%) and takes them both from $1,200; the 25% applies to the $720 left.
n.3: $180 is the amount spent on supplies, not the amount left.

MA.q: Jordan earns $2,850 per month. He puts 12% of his earnings into a retirement account and 8% into a savings account. How much of his monthly earnings is left after both?
MA.w: Both are percents of the same $2,850, so they add: 12% + 8% = 20% set aside, leaving 80%. 0.80 × 2,850 = $2,280.

n.0: This subtracts the 12% retirement contribution but not the 8% savings.
n.2: This subtracts the 8% savings but not the 12% retirement contribution.
n.3: This is the 20% set aside, not the amount left.

MA.q: An order is for 0.45 g of a medication. The oral suspension contains 150 mg per 5 mL. How many milliliters should be given?
MA.w: Convert: 0.45 g × 1,000 = 450 mg. Desired ÷ have × quantity: 450 ÷ 150 × 5 = 3 × 5 = 15 mL.

n.0: This inverts the ratio: 150 ÷ 450 × 5 = 1.7 mL.
n.1: This converts 0.45 g to 4,500 mg. Grams to milligrams is × 1,000, so 0.45 g = 450 mg.
n.2: This stops at desired ÷ have (450 ÷ 150 = 3) and does not multiply by the 5 mL quantity.

MA.q: A water test shows that 0.024 of a sample is sediment. Which fraction, in lowest terms, is equal to 0.024?
MA.w: 0.024 has three decimal places: 24/1,000. The GCF of 24 and 1,000 is 8, so 24/1,000 = 3/125. Check: 3 ÷ 125 = 0.024.

n.0: 6/25 = 0.24; it writes 24 over 100 instead of 1,000.
n.1: 3/250 = 0.012; it divides 24 by 8 but 1,000 by 4.

MA.q: Evaluate 40 ÷ (2 + 3) × 4 - 3². Enter the number only.
MA.w: Parentheses: 2 + 3 = 5. Exponent: 3² = 9. Division and multiplication left to right: 40 ÷ 5 = 8, then 8 × 4 = 32. Subtraction: 32 - 9 = 23.

MA.q: The value of √90 lies between which pair of numbers?
MA.w: 9² = 81 and 10² = 100. Since 81 < 90 < 100, √90 is between 9 and 10 (about 9.49).

n.0: 9² = 81, which is already less than 90, so √90 is greater than 9.
n.1: 81 and 100 are the perfect squares on either side of 90; √90 itself is about 9.49, which lies between their square roots, 9 and 10.
n.2: 10² = 100, which is already greater than 90, so √90 is less than 10.

MA.q: A patient takes 750 mg of a medication in the morning and 1.5 g at night. What is the ratio of the morning dose to the night dose, in lowest terms?
MA.w: Match units first: 1.5 g = 1,500 mg. Morning to night: 750:1,500. Divide both by 750: 1:2.

n.0: This reverses the order. The morning dose is named first, so it comes first.
n.1: This converts 1.5 g to 15,000 mg. Grams to milligrams is × 1,000, so 1.5 g = 1,500 mg.
n.2: This divides 750 by 1.5 without converting grams to milligrams.

MA.q: A parent reports that a child's temperature was 104 °F at home. Convert this temperature to degrees Celsius. Enter your answer in degrees Celsius as a whole number.

tr.26: Multiplied by 5/9 first and then subtracted 32 (104 x 5/9 = 57.8; 57.8 - 32 = 25.8).
tr.72: Subtracted 32 but did not multiply by 5/9.

MA.q: A patient drank 1 1/2 pints of water during a shift. Use 1 pint = 480 mL. How many milliliters did the patient drink?

n.0: This uses 960 mL, the value of a quart (2 pints), for each pint.
n.1: This uses 240 mL, the value of 1 cup, instead of the 480 mL pint given in the stem.
n.3: This uses 500 mL per pint, a rounded value some texts give; use the 480 mL printed in the stem.

MA.q: A medication infuses at 400 mcg per minute. How many milligrams does the patient receive in 1 hour?

n.1: This divides 24,000 mcg by 10,000 instead of 1,000.
n.2: This divides 24,000 mcg by 100 instead of 1,000.
n.3: 0.4 mg is one minute's amount (400 mcg); multiply by the 60 minutes in an hour.

MA.q: Which is the correct way to write 6.045 in words?
o: six and four hundred five thousandths
MA.w: Read the digits after the point as a whole number (045 = forty-five) and name the place of the last digit (thousandths): six and forty-five thousandths.

n.1: Four hundred five thousandths is 6.405; the 0 comes right after the point in 6.045.
n.2: Forty-five ten-thousandths is 6.0045, one place too far right.
n.3: Forty-five hundredths is 6.45; the last digit of 6.045 is in the thousandths place.

MA.q: A nurse has 9/10 of a bottle of hand sanitizer and uses 2/3 of a full bottle during a shift. What fraction of a bottle is left?

n.0: 7/10 subtracts the numerators (9 - 2) and keeps the denominator 10 without a common denominator.
n.1: 17/30 renames 2/3 as 10/30; to reach thirtieths the numerator 2 must be multiplied by 10, giving 20/30.
n.3: 3/10 takes 2/3 of the 9/10 left (6/10), but the nurse used 2/3 of a full bottle.

MA.q: On a dosage calculation quiz, Marcus answered 0.64 of the items correctly. Which fraction, written in lowest terms, is equal to 0.64?
MA.w: 0.64 has two decimal places, so write it over 100: 64/100. The GCF of 64 and 100 is 4, so 64/100 = 16/25.

n.0: 32/50 equals 0.64, but it is not in lowest terms; 32 and 50 still share a factor of 2.
n.1: This writes 0.64 over 10 instead of 100 (64/10 = 32/5 = 6.4).
n.2: This divides 64 by 4 but 100 by 5, so the value changes: 16/20 = 0.8.

MA.q: A pharmacy technician needs a value that is greater than 1/3 but less than 3/8. Which value lies between 1/3 and 3/8?
MA.w: 1/3 = 0.333... and 3/8 = 0.375. 0.35 is greater than 0.333... and less than 0.375, so it lies between them.

n.0: 0.38 is greater than 3/8 = 0.375, so it is above the range.
n.2: 0.33 is less than 1/3 = 0.333..., so it is below the range.
n.3: 2/5 = 0.4, which is greater than 3/8.

MA.q: A child has a fever of 102.2 °F. The pediatric chart records temperatures in degrees Celsius. What is the child's temperature in degrees Celsius? Round to the nearest tenth if necessary, and enter the number only.

tr.126.4: Subtracted 32 and then multiplied by 9/5 instead of 5/9.

MA.q: On a state map, 1.5 inches represents 40 miles. Two towns are 5.25 inches apart on the map. What is the actual distance between the two towns?
MA.w: Set up 1.5/40 = 5.25/d. Cross-multiply: 1.5d = 210, so d = 140 miles.

n.0: This rounds 26.67 miles per inch to 27 before multiplying. Round only at the end.
n.1: This multiplies 5.25 by 40 as if 1 inch represented 40 miles.
n.2: This multiplies 40 by 1.5 to get 60 miles per inch instead of dividing.

MA.q: A disinfectant is mixed so that 3/40 of the final solution is concentrate and the rest is water. What percent of the final solution is concentrate? Enter the number only, without the percent sign.

tr.0.075: Left the answer as a decimal instead of a percent.
tr.0.75: Moved the decimal point only 1 place right.
tr.92.5: Found the percent that is water (100 - 7.5) instead of concentrate.

MA.w: 3/40 = 3 ÷ 40 = 0.075. Multiply by 100: 0.075 × 100 = 7.5, so 7.5% of the solution is concentrate.

MA.q: A pharmacy has 0.6 g of a powdered drug. Each dose uses 0.003 g. How many doses can be prepared from the powder?
MA.w: Move both decimal points 3 places right: 0.6 ÷ 0.003 = 600 ÷ 3 = 200 doses.

n.0: 0.0018 is 0.6 × 0.003; dividing the supply by the dose gives the number of doses.
n.2: 20 moves the decimal point in 0.6 only 2 places while moving 0.003 three places.
n.3: 2,000 moves the decimal point in 0.6 four places while moving 0.003 three places.

MA.q: Solve for x: 4(x - 3) = 2x + 10.
MA.w: Distribute: 4x - 12 = 2x + 10. Subtract 2x from both sides: 2x - 12 = 10. Add 12: 2x = 22. Divide by 2: x = 11. Check: 4(8) = 32 and 2(11) + 10 = 32.

n.0: This distributes the 4 to x only, giving 4x - 3 = 2x + 10, so 2x = 13.
n.1: Sign error when moving the constant: 4x - 12 = 2x + 10 gives 2x = 22, not 2x = -2.
n.3: This adds 2x to the left side instead of subtracting it, giving 6x - 12 = 10, so 6x = 22.

MA.q: Mia earns $18.40 per hour for her first 40 hours each week and 1.5 times that rate for every hour over 40. Last week she worked 46.5 hours. What was her total pay?

n.0: $1,283.40 pays all 46.5 hours at the overtime rate.
n.1: $855.60 pays all 46.5 hours at the regular rate.
n.2: $901.60 counts only 6 overtime hours instead of 6.5.

MA.q: An IV bag holds 1,000 mL. It infuses at a constant rate of r mL per hour, and after 8 hours, 280 mL remain in the bag. The equation 1,000 - 8r = 280 models the situation. What is r?
MA.w: 1,000 - 8r = 280. Subtract 1,000 from both sides: -8r = -720. Divide by -8: r = 90 mL per hour. Check: 8 × 90 = 720 mL infused, and 1,000 - 720 = 280 mL left.

n.0: Sign error: this adds 280 to 1,000, giving 8r = 1,280. The 280 mL left must be subtracted from 1,000.
n.1: This divides the amount remaining by 8 hours. The rate comes from the amount infused, 720 mL.
n.3: This divides the full 1,000 mL by 8 hours, as if the bag had emptied.

n.1: 3 4/9 subtracts the smaller fraction from the larger (7/9 - 3/9) instead of borrowing.
n.2: 2 2/9 borrows 9/9 but drops the original 3/9 (4 9/9 - 2 7/9).
n.3: 3 5/9 adds the borrowed 9/9 to the fraction but does not take 1 from the 5.

MA.q: A community clinic saw 1,248 patients in the first quarter of the year and 1,575 in the second quarter. Its goal for the first half of the year was 3,000 patients. How many more patients would the clinic have needed to meet its goal?
MA.w: Patients seen: 1,248 + 1,575 = 2,823. Shortfall: 3,000 - 2,823 = 177 patients.

n.0: 327 is how many more patients were seen in the second quarter than in the first.
n.1: 2,823 is the number of patients seen, not the number still needed.
n.2: 1,425 subtracts only the second quarter's patients from the goal.

MA.q: Four bandage rolls measure 2 3/8, 2.4, 2 5/12 and 2.38 meters. Which roll is longest?
MA.w: All four have 2 whole meters, so compare the parts: 3/8 = 0.375, 0.4, 5/12 = 0.4166... and 0.38. The greatest is 0.4166..., so 2 5/12 meters is longest.

n.0: 2 3/8 = 2.375, the shortest of the four rolls.
n.2: 2.4 = 2.400 is less than 2 5/12 = 2.4166...; the fraction must be converted before comparing.
n.3: 2.38 = 2.380 is less than 2.400 and 2.4166...; more digits do not make a decimal larger.

MA.q: A printer in a clinic prints 18 pages in 45 seconds. At this rate, how many pages can it print in 4 minutes?
MA.w: Convert first: 4 minutes = 240 seconds. Set up 18/45 = p/240. Cross-multiply: 45p = 4,320, so p = 96 pages.

n.0: This treats 18 pages as the number printed per minute, multiplying 18 by 4.
n.1: This divides 45 by 18 and multiplies by 4, which inverts the rate.
n.3: This mixes units, comparing 4 minutes with 45 seconds without converting 4 minutes to 240 seconds.

MA.q: Jordan finishes a 10-kilometer charity run in 50 minutes. Use 1 mile = 1.6 kilometers. What was Jordan's average speed for the run in miles per hour?

n.0: 12 is the speed in kilometers per hour; convert 10 km to 6.25 mi first.
n.2: This multiplies 10 km by 1.6; kilometers to miles means dividing by 1.6.
n.3: This treats 50 minutes as 0.5 hour; 50 min = 50/60 of an hour.

MA.q: A school nurse finds that a supply order is 2 3/5 times the size of last month's order. Which percentage is equivalent to 2 3/5?
MA.w: Convert the mixed number to a decimal: 3/5 = 0.6, so 2 3/5 = 2.6. Multiply by 100: 2.6 = 260%.

n.0: 60% is the value of 3/5 by itself; the whole number 2 (200%) was dropped.
n.1: This reads 2 3/5 as the digits 2.35 instead of converting 3/5 to 0.6.
n.3: 26% = 0.26. The decimal point in 2.6 was moved only 1 place right.

MA.q: A nurse begins a 12.5-hour shift at 6:45 p.m. She stays 40 minutes after the shift ends to finish charting. At what time does she leave?
MA.w: 12.5 hours = 12 hours 30 minutes. 6:45 p.m. + 12 hours = 6:45 a.m.; + 30 minutes = 7:15 a.m. (end of shift); + 40 minutes = 7:55 a.m.

n.1: This reads 12.5 hours as 12 hours 50 minutes; 0.5 hour is 30 minutes.
n.2: Twelve and a half hours after 6:45 p.m. is the next morning, so the time is a.m.
n.3: This is when the shift ends; the 40 minutes of charting must be added.

MA.q: Solve for x: (x + 3)/5 = (x - 1)/3.
MA.w: Cross-multiply: 3(x + 3) = 5(x - 1). Distribute: 3x + 9 = 5x - 5. Subtract 3x and add 5: 14 = 2x, so x = 7. Check: 10/5 = 2 and 6/3 = 2.

n.0: This cross-multiplies without distributing: 3x + 3 = 5x - 1 instead of 3(x + 3) = 5(x - 1).
n.2: Sign error in the last step: -2x = -14 gives a positive x.
n.3: This distributes on the left but not on the right: 3x + 9 = 5x - 1.

MA.q: A roll holds 8 1/5 meters of gauze. A nurse cuts off 2 1/2 meters. How many meters are left on the roll?

n.0: 5 1/2 borrows 10/10 but drops the original 2/10 (7 10/10 - 2 5/10).
n.1: 6 3/10 subtracts the smaller fraction from the larger (5/10 - 2/10) instead of borrowing.
n.2: 6 7/10 adds the borrowed 10/10 to the fraction but does not take 1 from the 8.

MA.q: A 12-pack of bottled water costs $5.40, and a 30-pack of the same bottles costs $12.90. How much less per bottle does the 30-pack cost than the 12-pack?

n.0: $0.43 is the price per bottle in the 30-pack, not the difference.
n.1: $0.20 places the decimal point one place too far right in the difference.
n.3: $7.50 is the difference between the package prices, not the per-bottle prices.

MA.q: A patient on a fluid restriction weighed 68.4 kg on Monday and 67.85 kg on Friday. How many kilograms did the patient lose between the two weigh-ins? Enter the number of kilograms only.

tr.1.45: Subtracted the smaller digit from the larger in each column instead of borrowing.
tr.136.25: Added the weights instead of subtracting.

MA.w: Line up the decimal points and write 68.4 as 68.40: 68.40 - 67.85 = 0.55 kg.

MA.q: A nurse works from 0645 to 1920 with a 30-minute unpaid break. How much paid time does she work?
MA.w: 1920 - 0645: borrow 1 hour, 18 h 80 min - 6 h 45 min = 12 h 35 min. Minus the 30-minute break: 12 h 5 min.

n.0: This subtracts 20 from 45 without borrowing (13 h 25 min) before taking off the break.
n.1: 12 h 35 min is the whole time at work; the 30-minute break is unpaid.
n.3: This borrows 100 minutes (1920 - 0645 = 1275, read as 13 h 15 min) before taking off the break.

MA.q: Which number is prime?
MA.w: 53 has exactly two factors, 1 and 53: it is not divisible by 2, 3, 5 or 7 (7 × 7 = 49 and 8 × 8 = 64, so no larger prime needs checking).

n.0: 91 = 7 × 13, so it is composite.
n.1: 57 = 3 × 19 (digit sum 12 is divisible by 3), so it is composite.
n.3: 51 = 3 × 17 (digit sum 6 is divisible by 3), so it is composite.

MA.q: To divide a dose by 2 2/5, a nurse multiplies by the reciprocal of 2 2/5 instead. What is the reciprocal of 2 2/5?
MA.w: First write the mixed number as an improper fraction: 2 2/5 = (2 × 5 + 2)/5 = 12/5. Then flip it: the reciprocal is 5/12. Check: 12/5 × 5/12 = 1.

n.0: 12/5 is 2 2/5 written as an improper fraction; it has not been flipped.
n.1: This reads 2 2/5 as 22/5 before flipping; the improper fraction is 12/5.
n.2: This flips the fraction part 2/5 and drops the whole number.

MA.q: A saline solution is 0.9% sodium chloride by mass. How many grams of sodium chloride are in 500 grams of the solution?
MA.w: 0.9% = 0.009. Part = 0.009 × 500 = 4.5 g of sodium chloride.

n.0: This uses 0.09 for 0.9%. Moving the decimal two places left gives 0.009.
n.1: This moves the decimal point three places left; 0.9% = 0.009.
n.2: This treats 0.9% as 0.9, which is 90%.

MA.q: Write 2,048 in Roman numerals.
MA.w: 2,000 = MM, 40 = XL, 8 = VIII. Together: MMXLVIII.

n.1: MMLXVIII = 2,068; LX is 60, and 40 is XL.
n.2: 8 is written VIII; subtracting two I's from X is not standard.
n.3: X may not repeat four times; 40 is written XL.

MA.q: A 500 mL IV bag is hung. After 2 hours, 36% of it has infused. In the next hour, 1/4 of the remaining volume infuses. How many milliliters are left?
MA.w: First 2 hours: 0.36 × 500 = 180 mL, leaving 320 mL. Next hour: 1/4 × 320 = 80 mL, leaving 320 - 80 = 240 mL.

n.1: 80 mL is the amount infused in the third hour, not the amount left.
n.2: 195 takes 1/4 of the full 500 mL (125) instead of 1/4 of the 320 mL remaining.
n.3: 320 mL is the volume left after 2 hours, one step short of the answer.

MA.q: A hospital cornerstone is engraved MCMLXIV. In what year was the cornerstone laid?

n.0: This reads IV as 6; I before V is subtracted, so IV = 4.
n.2: This reads CM as 1,100 instead of 1,000 - 100 = 900.
n.3: This reads LX as 40; L before X is added, so LX = 60 (40 is XL).

MA.q: A hospital's indoor walking path is 750 meters long. As part of a rehabilitation plan, a patient walks 4 laps of the path each day for 5 days. How many kilometers does the patient walk in total over the 5 days?
MA.w: Total meters = 750 × 4 × 5 = 15,000 m. Meters to kilometers: divide by 1,000, so 15,000 m = 15 km.

n.0: This divides 15,000 m by 100 instead of 1,000.
n.1: This divides 15,000 m by 10,000; 1 km = 1,000 m.
n.3: This is one day's distance (750 × 4 = 3,000 m = 3 km); the plan covers 5 days.

MA.q: A home health nurse drives 24 miles at an average of 32 miles per hour to reach her first patient, then 35 miles at 60 miles per hour to reach her second. What is her total driving time?
MA.w: Time = distance ÷ speed. Leg 1: 24 ÷ 32 = 0.75 h = 45 min. Leg 2: 35 ÷ 60 = 7/12 h = 35 min. Total: 45 + 35 = 80 min = 1 h 20 min.

n.0: 1 h 33 min reads 1.33 hours as 1 hour 33 minutes; 0.33 h is about 20 minutes.
n.1: 1 h 17 min divides the total distance by the average of the two speeds (59 ÷ 46); the legs must be timed separately.
n.3: 45 min is the time for the first leg only.

MA.q: Solve the proportion (x + 2)/9 = 4/6.
MA.w: Cross-multiply: 6(x + 2) = 4 × 9 = 36. Divide by 6: x + 2 = 6. Subtract 2: x = 4. Check: 6/9 = 2/3 and 4/6 = 2/3.

n.0: This flips the second ratio, solving (x + 2)/9 = 6/4.
n.1: This cross-multiplies without distributing: 6x + 2 = 36 instead of 6(x + 2) = 36.
n.2: This uses addition: 9 is 3 more than 6, so it adds 3 to 4. Proportions scale by multiplying.

MA.q: A patient in a weight-management program weighed 182 pounds at week 2 and 173 pounds at week 6. On average, how many pounds per week did the patient lose over this period?
MA.w: Weight lost: 182 - 173 = 9 pounds. Time: week 2 to week 6 is 6 - 2 = 4 weeks. Rate: 9 ÷ 4 = 2.25 pounds per week.

n.0: This divides the 9-pound loss by 6, the week number, instead of the 4 weeks that passed.
n.2: This divides the 9-pound loss by 2, the starting week number, instead of the 4 weeks that passed.
n.3: This divides the weeks by the pounds (4 ÷ 9), which inverts the rate.

AP.q: A 45-year-old patient with obesity has high blood glucose even though his pancreas still produces insulin. Which description best fits his condition?
o: Type 1 diabetes mellitus caused by beta-cell destruction
Type 2 diabetes mellitus caused by insulin resistance
Diabetes insipidus caused by a lack of ADH
Type 1 diabetes mellitus caused by insulin resistance
AP.w: Type 2 diabetes mellitus is mainly insulin resistance (with a relative deficiency) and is linked to obesity and inactivity; insulin is still produced.

n.0: Beta-cell destruction leaves no insulin, but this patient still produces insulin.
n.2: Diabetes insipidus is an ADH problem causing dilute urine; it does not raise blood glucose.
n.3: Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune destruction of beta cells; insulin resistance defines type 2.

AP.q: The ventral body cavity is subdivided by a dome-shaped muscle that contracts during breathing. Which two cavities does the diaphragm separate?
AP.w: The diaphragm separates the thoracic cavity (lungs, heart) above from the abdominopelvic cavity below.

n.0: The pleural and pericardial cavities both lie within the thoracic cavity above the diaphragm.
n.1: The abdominal and pelvic cavities are continuous, both within the abdominopelvic cavity below the diaphragm.
n.2: The cranial and vertebral cavities form the dorsal cavity; the diaphragm is part of the ventral cavity.

AP.q: The first heart sound, S1 ("lub"), is produced by which event in the cardiac cycle?
o: Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the start of diastole
Closure of the tricuspid and mitral valves as ventricular systole begins
Opening of the aortic and pulmonary valves as the ventricles eject
Contraction of the atria at the end of ventricular filling
AP.w: S1 ("lub") is the sound of the atrioventricular valves (tricuspid and mitral) closing as the ventricles begin to contract. S2 ("dub") is the semilunar valves closing.

n.0: Closure of the semilunar valves at the start of diastole produces S2 ("dub"), not S1.
n.2: Normal heart sounds come from valves closing, not opening.
n.3: Atrial contraction tops up ventricular filling but is not the source of S1.

AP.q: The renal corpuscle is the part of the nephron where blood is first filtered. Which two structures together make up the renal corpuscle?
AP.w: The renal corpuscle is the glomerulus (capillary tuft) surrounded by the glomerular (Bowman's) capsule. Filtration happens there, not in the tubule.

n.0: The proximal convoluted tubule follows the capsule; it is part of the renal tubule, not the corpuscle.
n.1: The nephron loop (loop of Henle) is part of the tubule and lies mainly in the medulla.
n.2: These arterioles supply and drain the glomerulus but are not the corpuscle itself.

AP.q: Autonomic motor fibers leave the spinal cord between vertebral levels T1 and L2. Which division do these fibers belong to, and what is one effect they produce?
o: Sympathetic; they slow digestion and urination
Parasympathetic; they stimulate digestion and urination
Parasympathetic; they slow the heart rate
AP.w: Two steps: outflow from T1 to L2 is the thoracolumbar, or sympathetic, division. Sympathetic effects include slowing digestion and urination, as well as dilating the bronchioles and pupils and raising the heart rate.

n.1: Stimulating digestion and urination is parasympathetic, and parasympathetic outflow is craniosacral, not thoracolumbar.
n.2: Slowing the heart is a parasympathetic effect, but parasympathetic outflow is craniosacral, not T1 to L2.
n.3: The division is right, but sympathetic stimulation dilates the bronchioles; constriction is parasympathetic.

AP.q: At the junction between a motor neuron and a skeletal muscle fiber, a neurotransmitter triggers contraction and is then broken down by an enzyme in the synaptic cleft. Which neurotransmitter is it?
AP.w: At the neuromuscular junction, motor neurons release acetylcholine, which is broken down in the synaptic cleft by acetylcholinesterase.

n.1: Glutamate is the main excitatory neurotransmitter of the CNS, not the transmitter released onto skeletal muscle.
n.2: Dopamine is a neurotransmitter of the brain, not the one released at the neuromuscular junction.
n.3: Norepinephrine is the main sympathetic effector neurotransmitter, not the transmitter at the neuromuscular junction.

AP.q: While jogging on a hot afternoon, a person's body temperature starts to rise. Which pair of skin responses is mainly responsible for releasing the excess heat?
o: Dermal vessels constrict; eccrine glands secrete sweat
Dermal vessels constrict; arrector pili muscles contract
Dermal vessels dilate; eccrine glands secrete sweat
Dermal vessels dilate; apocrine glands secrete sweat
AP.w: To lose heat, dermal blood vessels dilate so more warm blood reaches the surface, and eccrine glands secrete watery sweat that cools the skin as it evaporates.

n.0: Constriction of dermal vessels conserves heat, the opposite of what is needed here.
n.1: Vessel constriction and arrector pili contraction are heat-conserving responses to cold.
n.3: Apocrine glands in the axillae and groin respond mainly to stress and puberty; eccrine glands are the main thermoregulators.

AP.q: About a week after fertilization, the developing human implants in the endometrium of the uterus. Which stage implants, and how is it correctly described?
o: Blastocyst, a solid ball of cells made by cleavage
Morula, a hollow ball with a trophoblast layer
Blastocyst, a hollow ball with a trophoblast layer
Morula, a solid ball of cells made by cleavage
AP.w: Development runs zygote, cleavage, morula, blastocyst, implantation, embryo (to week 8), fetus (week 9 to birth). The blastocyst implants about a week after fertilization, and its trophoblast later forms part of the placenta and secretes hCG.

n.0: Blastocyst is the right stage, but it is hollow (a fluid-filled cavity ringed by trophoblast); the solid ball made by cleavage is the morula.
n.1: A hollow ball with a trophoblast layer is the blastocyst; the morula is a solid ball with no cavity or trophoblast, and it comes first.
n.3: The morula is the solid ball formed by cleavage, but it develops into a blastocyst before implantation; the morula does not implant.

AP.q: Swallowed food and inhaled air both travel through one region of the upper respiratory tract before their paths separate. Which structure is this shared passageway?
AP.w: The pharynx (throat) is shared by the respiratory and digestive tracts: air passes on to the larynx, while food passes behind it into the esophagus.

n.0: The trachea carries air only, from the larynx to the main bronchi; it lies in front of the esophagus.
n.1: The larynx (voice box) carries air only; the epiglottis covers it during swallowing so food does not enter.
n.3: The nasal cavity warms, humidifies and filters inhaled air; food does not normally pass through it.

AP.q: Which white blood cell is the largest in normal blood and leaves the bloodstream to become a macrophage in the tissues?
AP.w: Monocytes are the largest leukocytes. They circulate briefly, then enter the tissues and develop into macrophages, long-lived phagocytes that also present antigens.

n.0: Lymphocytes (B, T and NK cells) drive specific and antiviral defense; they do not become macrophages.
n.1: Neutrophils are the most numerous WBCs and the first phagocytes at an infection, but they do not develop into macrophages.
n.3: Basophils are the least numerous WBCs and release histamine and heparin; they are not macrophage precursors.

AP.q: The right and left hypochondriac regions are two of the nine abdominal regions. Based on the word parts, where do they lie?
AP.w: hypo- means below and chondr/o means cartilage, so the hypochondriac regions lie below the costal cartilages of the lower ribs, at the two sides of the top row of the nine regions.

n.0: Above the stomach describes the epigastric region (epi- upon, gastr/o stomach), the middle of the top row.
n.2: The region below the umbilical region is the hypogastric (pubic) region, the middle of the bottom row.
n.3: The regions beside the hip bones are the iliac (inguinal) regions of the bottom row.

AP.q: Which sequence names a structure at each of three successive levels of organization, listed from the lowest of the three levels to the highest?
o: Muscle cell, the heart, cardiac muscle tissue
AP.w: An epithelial cell is the cellular level, epithelial tissue is the tissue level, and the stomach (built from four tissue types) is the organ level: three successive levels in rising order.

n.0: This runs organ, organ system, organ. The small intestine is another organ, so the sequence drops back a level.
n.2: This runs chemical, tissue, cellular. The cell must come before the tissue.
n.3: This runs cell, organ, tissue. The tissue level must come before the organ level.

AP.q: After several hours of hiking without water, Grace becomes dehydrated and her ADH secretion rises. How does this change the urine her kidneys produce?
o: Smaller volume of more dilute urine
Smaller volume of more concentrated urine
Larger volume of urine containing more sodium
Larger volume of more dilute urine
AP.w: ADH (antidiuretic hormone) makes the collecting ducts reabsorb more water, so the kidneys produce a smaller volume of more concentrated urine.

n.0: Reabsorbing more water leaves the remaining urine more concentrated, not more dilute.
n.2: ADH reduces urine volume; increased sodium and water loss is the effect of ANP from the heart.
n.3: This is the effect of low ADH; ADH is anti-diuretic, so it reduces urine output.

AP.q: The diaphragm forms the floor of the thoracic cavity. Which statement correctly describes its position in anatomical position?
o: It is superior to the lungs and inferior to the stomach
It is inferior to the heart and superior to the liver
It is inferior to the stomach and superior to the bladder
It is superior to the heart and inferior to the trachea
AP.w: The diaphragm separates the thoracic cavity (heart, lungs) from the abdominopelvic cavity (liver, stomach). It lies below the heart and above the liver.

n.0: The lungs sit above the diaphragm and the stomach below it, so the diaphragm is inferior to the lungs and superior to the stomach.
n.2: The stomach lies below the diaphragm in the abdominal cavity, so the diaphragm is superior to the stomach.
n.3: The heart rests on the diaphragm, so the diaphragm is inferior to the heart.

AP.q: A person lifts a grocery bag by flexing the elbow. Which muscle acts as the antagonist to the prime mover during this movement?
AP.w: In elbow flexion the biceps brachii is the agonist (prime mover). The triceps brachii, which extends the elbow, is the antagonist: it relaxes and stretches as the biceps contracts.

n.0: The pectoralis major flexes, adducts and medially rotates the arm at the shoulder; it does not oppose elbow flexion.
n.1: The biceps brachii is the prime mover (agonist) of elbow flexion, not its antagonist.
n.2: The deltoid abducts the arm at the shoulder; it does not oppose elbow flexion.

AP.q: A patient's terminal ileum is removed because of disease, but the duodenum and jejunum are left in place. Absorption of which nutrient is most at risk after this surgery?
AP.w: Vitamin B12, bound to intrinsic factor from the stomach, is absorbed in the ileum. Removing the ileum therefore threatens B12 absorption even though the rest of the small intestine remains.

n.0: Glucose is absorbed mainly in the jejunum, which is still present.
n.2: Vitamin K is fat-soluble and is supplied partly by bacteria in the large intestine, which is untouched; uptake of B12 with intrinsic factor is the ileum's specific job.
n.3: Intrinsic factor and the ileum are linked to vitamin B12, not iron; confusing them is a classic trap.

AP.q: A student is sorting bones into the axial and appendicular divisions of the skeleton. Which of the following bones belongs to the axial skeleton?
AP.w: The axial skeleton (80 bones) is the skull, hyoid, auditory ossicles, vertebral column and rib cage. The pectoral girdle (clavicle, scapula) and the pelvic girdle (hip bones) belong to the appendicular skeleton.

n.0: The hip bones form the pelvic girdle, which is appendicular even though it joins the sacrum.
n.1: The clavicle is part of the pectoral girdle, which belongs to the appendicular skeleton.
n.3: The scapula is part of the pectoral girdle, which belongs to the appendicular skeleton.

AP.q: Arterioles throughout the body constrict while cardiac output stays the same. What happens to blood pressure, and why?
o: It stays the same, because cardiac output is unchanged
It rises, because the stroke volume of the heart increases
It rises, because peripheral resistance increases
It falls, because less blood reaches the capillaries
AP.w: Step 1: blood pressure depends on cardiac output and peripheral resistance. Step 2: arterioles control resistance, so narrowing them raises resistance; with cardiac output unchanged, blood pressure rises.

n.0: Pressure depends on resistance as well as cardiac output, so a rise in resistance raises it.
n.1: Stroke volume is unchanged here (cardiac output is the same); the rise comes from resistance.
n.3: Constriction raises arterial pressure even though capillary flow falls.

AP.q: Tendons attach skeletal muscles to bones and must resist strong pulling forces in one direction. Which tissue forms tendons?
AP.w: Tendons and ligaments are dense regular connective tissue: tightly packed collagen fibers run parallel to one another, resisting strong pull in one direction.

n.0: Dense irregular connective tissue has collagen fibers running in many directions, suited to pull from several directions (as in the dermis), not the parallel fibers of a tendon.
n.1: Areolar tissue is loose connective tissue with a loose, open arrangement of fibers; it does not withstand strong one-direction pull.
n.3: Skeletal muscle generates the pull; the tendon that transmits it to bone is connective tissue.

AP.q: After a car accident, a patient's ruptured spleen is surgically removed. Which normal function is most directly lost along with the spleen?
o: Absorbing dietary fats through lacteals in the intestine
Filtering lymph before it returns to the bloodstream
Maturing T lymphocytes before they enter circulation
Filtering blood and removing worn-out red blood cells
AP.w: The spleen, the largest lymphoid organ, filters blood rather than lymph: it removes old or damaged red blood cells and platelets and mounts immune responses to blood-borne antigens.

n.0: Lacteals in the intestinal villi absorb dietary fats; the spleen has no part in fat absorption.
n.1: Filtering lymph is the job of the lymph nodes; the spleen filters blood.
n.2: T lymphocytes mature in the thymus, not the spleen.

AP.q: When a skeletal muscle fiber is stimulated, calcium ions flood the sarcoplasm. To which protein do these calcium ions bind directly to begin the process of contraction?
AP.w: Ca²⁺ binds troponin on the thin filament. This shifts tropomyosin off the myosin-binding sites on actin, so myosin heads can form cross-bridges.

n.0: Tropomyosin is the strand that covers actin's binding sites; it is moved by troponin, not bound by Ca²⁺.
n.2: Actin carries the binding sites for myosin; calcium acts on troponin, which then uncovers those sites.
n.3: Myosin heads bind actin and ATP; calcium does not bind myosin to start skeletal muscle contraction.

AP.q: A person's diet lacks iodine, so the thyroid makes too little T3 and T4. Through negative feedback, what happens to TSH secretion and the thyroid gland?
o: TSH falls, and the thyroid enlarges
TSH rises, and the thyroid enlarges
TSH falls, and the thyroid shrinks
TSH rises, and the thyroid shrinks
AP.w: Low T3 and T4 remove the negative feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, so TRH and TSH rise. Constant TSH stimulation enlarges the thyroid, producing a goiter.

n.0: Falling TSH would leave the thyroid unstimulated; the goiter forms because TSH is high.
n.2: TSH falls when T3 and T4 are high; here they are low, so the brake on TSH is released.
n.3: TSH does rise, but continuous TSH stimulation makes the gland grow, not shrink.

AP.q: Which ribs are called floating ribs because they have no anterior attachment to the sternum, either directly or through costal cartilage?
AP.w: Ribs 1 to 7 are true ribs, each with its own costal cartilage to the sternum. Ribs 8 to 12 are false ribs: 8 to 10 attach through the cartilage of rib 7, and 11 and 12 are floating ribs with no anterior attachment.

n.0: Ribs 8 to 12 are the false ribs; within that group, 8 to 10 still attach indirectly, so they do not float.
n.2: Ribs 1 to 7 are true ribs that attach directly to the sternum by their own costal cartilage.
n.3: Ribs 8 to 10 are false ribs that reach the sternum indirectly through rib 7's costal cartilage.

AP.q: During surgery on the spinal cord, the surgeon separates the protective membranes one at a time. Which meningeal layer lies directly against the surface of the spinal cord?
AP.w: From outer to inner, the meninges are the dura mater, arachnoid mater and pia mater. The pia mater is the innermost layer, lying directly on the brain and spinal cord.

n.1: The arachnoid mater is the middle layer; the subarachnoid space beneath it holds cerebrospinal fluid.
n.2: The dura mater is the outermost, toughest meningeal layer.
n.3: The choroid plexus makes cerebrospinal fluid in the ventricles; it is not one of the meninges.

AP.q: Which type of tissue forms the intervertebral discs and the menisci of the knee, where it resists compression and absorbs shock between bones?
AP.w: Fibrocartilage is the strongest, most shock-absorbing cartilage, with thick collagen bundles. It forms the intervertebral discs, the knee menisci and the pubic symphysis.

n.0: Hyaline cartilage covers articular surfaces and forms costal cartilage and growth plates; it is not the disc or meniscus tissue.
n.1: Dense regular connective tissue forms tendons and ligaments, not the discs or menisci.
n.3: Elastic cartilage gives flexible support in the ear auricle and epiglottis.

AP.q: In the baroreceptor reflex that corrects a sudden rise in blood pressure, where are the receptors, and which brain region is the control center?
o: Carotid and aortic bodies; medulla oblongata
Carotid sinus and aortic arch; hypothalamus
Carotid sinus and aortic arch; medulla oblongata
AP.w: Baroreceptors (stretch receptors) in the carotid sinus and the aortic arch detect the rise in pressure and signal the medulla oblongata, which slows the heart and dilates vessels. The response reverses the change: negative feedback.

n.0: The medulla is the right control center, but the carotid and aortic bodies hold chemoreceptors that sense O2, CO2 and H+, not pressure.
n.1: The receptor sites are right, but blood pressure reflexes run through the medulla; the hypothalamus is the control center for temperature and water balance.
n.3: The carotid and aortic bodies are chemoreceptor sites, and the hypothalamus is not the control center for the baroreceptor reflex.

AP.q: Parietal cells in the stomach lining secrete hydrochloric acid, which keeps gastric pH very low. Which of the following is a role of this acid?
o: Binding vitamin B12 for uptake in the ileum
Emulsifying fat droplets so lipase can act
AP.w: Hydrochloric acid activates pepsinogen into pepsin, which begins protein digestion, and it kills many swallowed microbes.

n.0: Binding vitamin B12 is the role of intrinsic factor, the other product of parietal cells, not the acid.
n.1: Emulsifying fat is the job of bile salts in the duodenum, not stomach acid.
n.2: Trypsinogen is activated in the duodenum by the brush-border enzyme enteropeptidase (and then by trypsin itself), not by stomach acid.

AP.q: A toddler inhales a small bead, and an X-ray shows it lodged in one of the main bronchi. Which bronchus is it most likely in, and why?
o: The left, because it is wider and runs more vertically than the right
The right, because it is shorter, wider and more vertical than the left
The left, because the heart pushes the trachea toward the left side
The right, because it is narrower and so traps objects more easily
AP.w: The right main bronchus is shorter, wider and more vertical than the left, so it continues almost straight down from the trachea and aspirated objects usually lodge there.

n.0: This describes the right main bronchus, not the left; the left is longer, narrower and angled more horizontally around the heart.
n.2: The heart sits to the left and makes the left bronchus angle away more sharply, which makes the left side the less likely site.
n.3: Right side is correct, but the reason is wrong: the right main bronchus is wider, not narrower.

AP.q: Urination involves two sphincters around the urethra. Which statement correctly describes these sphincters?
o: Both are smooth muscle, and both are under involuntary control
Internal is smooth and involuntary; external is skeletal and voluntary
Both are skeletal muscle, and both are under voluntary control
Internal is skeletal and voluntary; external is smooth and involuntary
AP.w: The internal urethral sphincter is smooth muscle under involuntary control; the external urethral sphincter is skeletal muscle, so it can be voluntarily controlled.

n.0: The internal sphincter is smooth and involuntary, but the external sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary control.
n.2: The external sphincter is skeletal and voluntary, but the internal sphincter is smooth muscle and involuntary.
n.3: This reverses the two: the internal sphincter is the smooth, involuntary one.

AP.q: Two healthy adults have very different natural skin tones. Which difference between their skin best explains this?
o: The amount of melanin their melanocytes produce
The number of melanocytes in their stratum corneum
The number of melanocytes in their stratum basale
The amount of keratin made by their keratinocytes
AP.w: People have similar numbers of melanocytes; differences in natural skin color come mainly from how much melanin those melanocytes produce (with smaller contributions from carotene and hemoglobin).

n.1: Melanocytes are located in the stratum basale, not the dead stratum corneum.
n.2: Melanocyte numbers are similar between people; it is their melanin output that differs.
n.3: Keratin is a structural, waterproofing protein, not the main pigment behind skin tone.

BI.q: A neutrophil engulfs a bacterium, enclosing it in a vesicle. Which organelle then fuses with the vesicle and digests the bacterium using hydrolytic enzymes in an acidic interior?
BI.w: Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes in an acidic interior and digest engulfed bacteria, food particles and worn-out organelles.

n.0: The Golgi packages proteins and makes lysosomes, but it does not itself digest engulfed bacteria.
n.1: Smooth ER makes lipids and detoxifies drugs; it does not digest engulfed microbes.
n.2: Peroxisomes break down fatty acids and toxins and convert hydrogen peroxide with catalase; they are not the acidic digestive sacs.

BI.q: Oxygen moves from the alveoli, where its concentration is high, into lung capillary cells by passing directly through the phospholipid bilayer. Which transport process does this describe?
BI.w: Small nonpolar molecules such as O₂ and CO₂ cross the bilayer directly, from high to low concentration, with no protein and no ATP: simple diffusion.

n.0: Facilitated diffusion needs a channel or carrier protein. Oxygen is small and nonpolar, so it passes through the lipid bilayer itself.
n.1: Active transport uses ATP to move substances against a gradient. Oxygen is moving down its gradient.
n.3: Osmosis is the movement of water, not of a dissolved gas such as oxygen.

BI.q: Salad oil forms a separate layer on a water-based dressing. Which statement explains why the oil does not dissolve in the water?
o: Oil is polar, so its charges repel the charges of water.
Oil is ionic, so its ions bond too tightly to separate.
Oil is less dense, so it floats and cannot mix with water.
Oil is nonpolar, so it cannot hydrogen bond with water.
BI.w: Water dissolves polar and ionic substances (hydrophilic). Oils are nonpolar (hydrophobic) and cannot form hydrogen bonds with water, so they separate.

n.0: Polar substances dissolve in water; oils fail to dissolve because they are nonpolar.
n.1: Oils are not ionic, and ionic compounds such as salt dissolve readily in water.
n.2: Density explains why the layer sits on top, not why the oil fails to dissolve.

BI.q: A biology student is listing features that prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells have in common. Which feature belongs on the list?
o: Ribosomes that carry out protein synthesis
A nuclear envelope surrounding the DNA
Mitochondria that produce most of the ATP
BI.w: Both cell types have a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, DNA and ribosomes. Prokaryotic ribosomes are smaller than eukaryotic ones, but both make proteins.

n.1: A nuclear envelope belongs to eukaryotes. Prokaryotic DNA sits in a nucleoid region with no surrounding membrane.
n.2: Mitochondria are membrane-bound organelles, which prokaryotes lack.
n.3: Linear chromosomes packaged with histones are a eukaryotic feature. Prokaryotes usually have a single circular chromosome.

BI.q: A student writes that the Krebs cycle produces most of the ATP in aerobic cellular respiration. Which stage actually produces the most ATP per molecule of glucose?
BI.w: The electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae) uses NADH and FADH2 from earlier stages to make most of the ATP from each glucose.

n.0: Pyruvate oxidation releases CO₂ and makes NADH but produces little ATP directly.
n.1: Fermentation is anaerobic and yields only the 2 ATP from glycolysis.
n.2: Glycolysis nets 2 ATP per glucose, a small share of the total.

BI.q: A plant is given water containing a heavy isotope of oxygen. During photosynthesis, where will most of the heavy oxygen end up?
o: In the glucose the leaf produces
In the carbon dioxide it absorbs
In the chlorophyll of the thylakoids
In the oxygen gas the leaf releases
BI.w: Water is split in the light reactions, and its oxygen atoms are released as O2. The O2 from photosynthesis comes from water, not from CO2.

n.0: The oxygen in glucose comes from CO2 fixed in the Calvin cycle.
n.1: CO2 is taken in from the air; the labeled water does not become CO2.
n.2: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy; it does not collect oxygen from water.

BI.q: A segment of the DNA template strand reads 3'-TAC-5'. Which mRNA codon is transcribed from it, and what is that codon's role?
o: UAC, copied directly from the template
AUG, the start codon for methionine
AUG, a stop codon that ends translation
ATG, a codon read at the ribosome
BI.w: Base pairing gives T->A, A->U, C->G, so 3'-TAC-5' is transcribed into 5'-AUG-3'. AUG is the start codon and codes for methionine.

n.0: Transcription makes a complementary copy, not an identical one; UAC is the matching tRNA anticodon.
n.2: AUG is the start codon. The stop codons are UAA, UAG and UGA.
n.3: mRNA contains uracil, not thymine, so the codon cannot be ATG.

BI.q: A point mutation changes one amino acid in the sequence of a digestive enzyme, and the enzyme stops working. Which explanation is most likely?
o: The new amino acid removed the gene's stop codon.
The new amino acid blocked transcription of the gene.
The new amino acid kept mRNA from leaving the nucleus.
The new amino acid changed the folding and shape.
BI.w: The amino acid sequence (primary structure) determines how the chain folds into its 3-D shape, and shape determines function. One changed amino acid can alter the active site.

n.0: Stop codons are part of the mRNA, not the protein, so an amino acid cannot remove one.
n.1: A changed amino acid is a feature of the finished protein; it cannot act back on transcription of the gene.
n.2: The protein is made after mRNA leaves the nucleus, so its amino acids cannot affect mRNA export.

BI.q: A short segment of double-stranded DNA contains 4 guanine-cytosine pairs and 6 adenine-thymine pairs. How many hydrogen bonds hold its two strands together?
BI.w: Step 1: G-C pairs have 3 hydrogen bonds and A-T pairs have 2. Step 2: (4 x 3) + (6 x 2) = 12 + 12 = 24.

n.0: 30 counts every pair as having 3 hydrogen bonds; A-T pairs have 2.
n.1: 20 counts every pair as having 2 hydrogen bonds; G-C pairs have 3.
n.3: 26 swaps the bond numbers: (4 x 2) + (6 x 3) gives 26.

BI.q: After a meal, liver cells link many glucose molecules into glycogen. How is this process classified?
o: Anabolic: it builds a polymer and uses energy
Anabolic: it builds a polymer and releases energy
Catabolic: it builds a polymer and uses energy
Catabolic: it breaks bonds and releases energy
BI.w: Anabolism builds larger molecules from smaller ones and requires energy. Making glycogen from glucose is anabolic.

n.1: Building a polymer requires energy; releasing energy is a feature of catabolism.
n.2: Catabolism breaks molecules down; building glycogen is anabolism.
n.3: Glycogen synthesis builds, not breaks, bonds between glucose units.

BI.q: Butter is solid at room temperature, while olive oil is liquid. Which difference in their fatty acids best explains this?
o: Butter's fats contain more glycerol molecules per fatty acid.
Olive oil's fatty acids carry more hydrogen atoms per carbon.
Butter's fatty acids are mostly saturated and pack tightly together.
Butter's fatty acids have more C=C double bonds, which form kinks.
BI.w: Saturated fatty acids have no C=C double bonds, so their straight chains pack tightly and the fat is solid. Unsaturated fatty acids in oils have double bonds that kink the chains.

n.0: Every triglyceride has one glycerol and three fatty acids; the difference is saturation.
n.1: This is reversed: saturated fatty acids such as butter's carry the most hydrogen. Olive oil's C=C double bonds mean fewer hydrogens.
n.3: This is reversed: double bonds and kinks belong to unsaturated fats, which are liquid.

BI.q: Two parents are both carriers (Aa) of an autosomal recessive disorder. Their first three children are unaffected. What is the chance that their fourth child will be affected?
o: 1 in 2, since each parent carries one a allele
3 in 4, since that is the share expected to show the trait
1 in 16, using the product rule across two children
1 in 4, the same as for each of the earlier children
BI.w: Each fertilization is independent. For Aa x Aa, every child has a 1/4 chance of being aa, whatever happened with earlier children.

n.0: 1 in 2 is the chance a child is a carrier (Aa). An affected child needs a from both parents: 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4.
n.1: 3/4 is the chance a child is unaffected (AA or Aa), not affected.
n.2: The product rule gives the chance of two specified events together; the question asks about one child.

BI.q: A selectively permeable membrane separates a 2% sucrose solution on side A from a 10% sucrose solution on side B. Sucrose cannot cross the membrane. What net movement will occur?
o: Sucrose moves from side B to side A.
Neither water nor sucrose will move.
Water moves from side A to side B.
Water moves from side B to side A.
BI.w: Step 1: side B has the higher solute concentration, so it has the lower water concentration. Step 2: in osmosis water moves toward the higher solute concentration, so the net flow is from A to B.

n.0: The stem states sucrose cannot cross, and osmosis moves water rather than solute.
n.1: Water can still cross the membrane. The sucrose difference drives osmosis even though sucrose itself cannot move.
n.3: Water moves toward the side with more solute (B), not away from it.

BI.q: Under a microscope, a dividing cell shows condensing chromosomes, a forming spindle and a breaking-down nuclear envelope. Which phase is shown?
BI.w: In prophase the chromosomes condense, the spindle forms and the nuclear envelope breaks down.

n.0: In metaphase the chromosomes are already lined up at the cell equator.
n.2: In interphase the chromosomes are not condensed and no spindle is present.
n.3: In telophase nuclear envelopes re-form and chromosomes decondense, the reverse of this.

BI.q: Human DNA sequences match chimpanzee DNA far more closely than mouse DNA. Which line of evidence for evolution does this comparison provide?
BI.w: Similarity in DNA and protein sequences is molecular evidence: more closely related species share more of their sequences.

n.0: The fossil record is preserved remains in rock layers, not DNA comparisons.
n.1: Comparative embryology compares early embryos, not DNA sequences.
n.3: Biogeography is the distribution of species across places on Earth.

BI.q: A student says cellular respiration is the same as breathing. Which statement best corrects the student?
